LLM foundations · decisions

Benchmarks, arenas and choosing models with evidence

Every model launch comes with a table of benchmark scores. Interviewers expect you to know what the common benchmarks measure, why they mislead, and how you'd choose a model for your own task instead.

Benchmark familyMeasuresWatch out for
MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GPQAKnowledge and reasoning on multiple-choice exam questions (GPQA: graduate-level science)Saturated at the top; contamination (questions seen in training)
Math (GSM8K, MATH, AIME-style)Multi-step mathsOlder sets saturated; reasoning-effort settings change scores
Coding (HumanEval, SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench)Writing code; fixing real GitHub issues; working in a terminalScores depend heavily on the agent harness used, not just the model
Tool use and agents (BFCL, τ-bench / tau-bench, others)Function-calling accuracy; multi-turn agent tasks with tools and policiesClosest to agent work, but your tools and policies differ
Long context (needle-in-a-haystack, RULER-style)Finding and using facts in long inputsRetrieval of one fact is easier than reasoning over many
Embeddings (MTEB)Retrieval, clustering, classification across many datasetsDomain mismatch; check the retrieval sub-scores in your language
Human preference arenas (LMArena)Which answer people prefer in blind pairwise votes (Elo-style rating)Favours style and length; not your users or tasks

Why public scores aren't your decision

  • Contamination: test questions leak into training data, inflating scores.
  • Harness effects: agent benchmarks measure model + prompt + tools + loop; a different harness changes rankings.
  • Settings: reasoning effort, temperature and sampling count (pass@1 vs pass@k) are often different between vendors' tables.
  • Distribution: your tickets, schemas and documents are not in any benchmark.

Reasoning vs instruct models

Instruct (non-reasoning) models
Answer directly. Fast and cheap. Best for extraction, classification, routing, rewriting, summarising.
Reasoning models
Produce internal thinking tokens before answering, controlled by an effort or budget setting. Better for planning, debugging, complex SQL and multi-step tool use; slower and pricier because thinking is billed as output.
In practice
Many current models do both, with a switch or effort level. Set effort per step: low for routing and grading, high for planning.

Why the chat app answers better than your API call

Consumer chat apps add a long hidden system prompt, tools (search, code execution), memory and sometimes higher reasoning effort. A bare API call has none of that. If API output looks worse, compare like with like: write a real system prompt, give the same tools, and set the same reasoning settings.

Choose with your own evidence

model_bakeoff.py: same cases, several models, quality + latency + cost in one table (pass in real call functions)Python
import statistics, time

def bakeoff(models: dict, cases: list[dict], grade, price_per_m: dict) -> list[dict]:
    """models: name -> fn(prompt) returning (text, input_tokens, output_tokens)."""
    rows = []
    for name, call in models.items():
        scores, latencies, cost = [], [], 0.0
        for case in cases:
            t = time.perf_counter()
            text, tin, tout = call(case["prompt"])
            latencies.append(time.perf_counter() - t)
            scores.append(grade(text, case))
            pin, pout = price_per_m[name]
            cost += tin / 1e6 * pin + tout / 1e6 * pout
        rows.append({"model": name, "accuracy": round(sum(scores) / len(scores), 2),
                     "p50_s": round(statistics.median(latencies), 3),
                     "cost_per_1k_requests": round(cost / len(cases) * 1000, 2)})
    return sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (-r["accuracy"], r["cost_per_1k_requests"]))

cases = [{"prompt": "classify: OutOfMemoryError", "label": "memory"}, {"prompt": "classify: AccessDenied", "label": "permissions"}]
fake = {"small": lambda p: ("memory" if "Memory" in p else "other", 40, 3),
        "large": lambda p: ("memory" if "Memory" in p else "permissions", 40, 3)}
for r in bakeoff(fake, cases, lambda text, c: text == c["label"], {"small": (0.25, 1.25), "large": (3.0, 15.0)}):
    print(r)
OutputOutput
{'model': 'large', 'accuracy': 1.0, 'p50_s': 0.0, 'cost_per_1k_requests': 0.17}
{'model': 'small', 'accuracy': 0.5, 'p50_s': 0.0, 'cost_per_1k_requests': 0.01}

Pick the cheapest model that clears your quality bar on your cases, then re-run the bake-off when new models arrive. Bedrock model evaluation jobs can run the same comparison as a managed service.

Interview: How do you use benchmarks when choosing a model?

"As a shortlist only. I know what they measure: MMLU and GPQA for knowledge and reasoning, SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench for coding agents, BFCL and tau-bench for tool use, MTEB for embeddings, LMArena for human preference. I also know why they mislead: contamination, different harnesses and reasoning settings, and a distribution unlike my data. So I shortlist two or three models, run my own eval set through each with the same prompts and tools, and compare accuracy, p95 latency and cost per request, then pick the cheapest model that meets the bar, with reasoning effort set per step."

LLM foundations · decisions

Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning

There are four ways to make a model better at your task. Interviewers ask this as "when would you fine-tune?", and the expected answer is "rarely, and last".

Problem you seeRight toolWhy
Model doesn't know your company's facts or they change oftenRAGKnowledge lives in documents you can update in minutes; answers can cite sources
Model needs live data or must take actionsTools / agentsQuery the system of record instead of baking data into weights
Output format, tone or style is wrongPrompt + examples, then fine-tuneBehaviour problems are what fine-tuning is good at
A narrow task at huge volume is too slow or costly on a big modelFine-tune / distil a small modelA tuned small model can match a large one on one task for a fraction of the cost
Specialised vocabulary the model keeps misreadingGlossary in prompt → fine-tune if it persistsTry the cheap fix first

One line to remember: RAG changes what the model knows; fine-tuning changes how the model behaves. They're not rivals, and mature systems sometimes use both.

Fine-tuning words you should recognise

Full fine-tuning
Update all weights. Expensive; needs lots of data; rare for LLM apps.
LoRA / PEFT
Freeze the model and train small low-rank adapter matrices (well under 1% of the parameters). Cheap, fast, and adapters can be swapped per task. The default method today.
QLoRA
LoRA on a 4-bit quantised base model so it fits on one GPU.
Distillation
A large "teacher" model labels data; a small "student" model is trained on those labels. Bedrock offers managed model distillation.
Quantisation
Store weights in fewer bits (8 or 4 instead of 16) to cut memory and cost with a small quality loss.
Catastrophic forgetting
Tuning on a narrow task makes the model worse at everything else. Mitigate with adapters and mixed data.
Instruction data format
JSONL rows of prompt/completion (or message lists). Quality and consistency of these rows matter more than quantity.
On AWS

Bedrock supports customising some models (fine-tuning, distillation) and importing your own weights with Custom Model Import. SageMaker AI is the route when you need full control of training (LoRA on open models, your own containers). Customised Bedrock models have their own hosting and pricing terms, so cost them before you start.

Interview: When would you fine-tune instead of using RAG?

"I'd start with prompting and few-shot examples, then RAG if the gap is knowledge. I'd consider fine-tuning when the gap is behaviour that prompts can't fix reliably: a strict output style, a domain-specific classification, or a narrow high-volume task where a tuned small model can replace a large one and cut cost and latency. Preconditions: a few hundred to a few thousand high-quality labelled examples, an eval set that shows prompting has plateaued, and a plan to retrain when the base model is retired. I wouldn't fine-tune to add facts that change, because retraining for every document update is slow and you lose citations. I'd use LoRA rather than full fine-tuning."

Interview: What is LoRA, in simple terms?

"Instead of updating a huge weight matrix W, LoRA freezes W and learns two small matrices A and B whose product is a low-rank update, so the effective weight is W + BA. With rank 8 or 16 that's a tiny number of trainable parameters, so training is fast, needs little memory, and the result is a small adapter file you can load on top of the base model or swap per task. Quality is usually close to full fine-tuning for task adaptation."

Calling LLMs on AWS

Bedrock APIs and endpoints map

Bedrock has two inference endpoints and five API shapes. Interviewers increasingly ask "Converse or Invoke or the OpenAI-compatible API, and why?" This lesson gives you the map.

Which one should you use?

SituationUseWhy
New AWS-native app, want to switch models freelyConverse on bedrock-runtimeSame request/response for every chat model; tool use, documents, images, Guardrails all built in. Most frameworks (LangChain ChatBedrockConverse, Strands BedrockModel, LlamaIndex BedrockConverse) use it underneath.
Need a provider-specific feature not yet in Converse, or embeddings / imagesInvokeModelRaw provider JSON; you handle each provider's format.
Existing OpenAI SDK code to migrateChat Completions or Responses (bedrock-runtime recommended; bedrock-mantle also supported)Change OPENAI_BASE_URL and use a Bedrock API key.
Want stored conversation state, background jobs or server-side tools (web search, code interpreter)Responses API on bedrock-mantleOnly mantle runs background requests and server-side tools.
Anthropic-native features and SDKMessages APIClaude's own format, on either endpoint.

Authentication

IAM / SigV4
The default for boto3 and AWS SDKs. Use roles in Lambda, Glue, ECS, AgentCore. Permissions like bedrock:InvokeModel, bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream (Converse uses the same actions).
Bedrock API keys
Bearer tokens for quick starts and the OpenAI SDK. Short-term keys are preferred; treat long-term keys like passwords and put them in Secrets Manager.
Mantle permissions
Inference on bedrock-mantle authorises bedrock-mantle:CreateInference.

Inference profiles and Regions

Many models are called through a cross-Region inference profile (IDs start with us., eu., apac., global.) that spreads load across Regions for capacity. Geographic profiles keep data inside that geography; global. profiles may process anywhere. If you have data-residency rules, choose a geographic profile and say so in interviews.

Interview: Converse vs InvokeModel?

"Converse gives one message-based schema across all chat models, with tool use, system prompts, documents and Guardrails as first-class fields, and a consistent usage and stop-reason format. Switching from Claude to Nova or Llama is a model ID change. InvokeModel sends the provider's native body, so you get every provider-specific parameter, but you write a different payload and parser per provider. I default to Converse and drop to Invoke for embeddings, image models or a feature Converse doesn't expose yet."

Interview: What is Bedrock Mantle?

"Mantle is AWS's distributed inference engine behind many Bedrock models, especially open-weight ones, and it has its own endpoint, bedrock-mantle.{region}.api.aws. It exposes OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs and the Anthropic Messages API, so you can point the OpenAI SDK at Bedrock by changing the base URL and key. Its Responses API supports stored conversation state with previous_response_id, background (async) inference and server-side tools. AWS still recommends bedrock-runtime for new apps, which now also serves the Responses and Chat Completions shapes, synchronously and with Guardrails and cross-Region profiles."

Calling LLMs on AWS

Converse API in depth

Every framework on AWS ends up calling Converse. Learn its request and response shape by heart and every framework becomes easier to debug.

Request shape

Converse request, annotated (// comments are notes, not valid JSON)JSON
{
  "modelId": "us.anthropic.claude-...",          // or an inference profile ARN
  "system":   [{"text": "You are a concise AWS data engineering assistant."}],
  "messages": [
    {"role": "user",      "content": [{"text": "What is a Glue DPU?"}]},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "A unit of compute: 4 vCPU and 16 GB."}]},
    {"role": "user",      "content": [{"text": "How many does G.2X use?"}]}
  ],
  "inferenceConfig": {"maxTokens": 512, "temperature": 0.2, "topP": 0.9},
  "toolConfig": {...},                           // optional: tools the model may call
  "guardrailConfig": {...},                      // optional: apply a Bedrock Guardrail
  "additionalModelRequestFields": {...}          // optional: provider-specific extras
}

Messages alternate user/assistant. Each message has a list of content blocks: text, image, document, toolUse, toolResult, reasoningContent, cachePoint.

A complete, reusable client

converse_basics.pyPython
import os, boto3
from botocore.config import Config

brt = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name=os.getenv("AWS_REGION", "us-east-1"),
                   config=Config(retries={"max_attempts": 8, "mode": "adaptive"}, read_timeout=300))
MODEL = os.environ["BEDROCK_MODEL_ID"]

def ask(question: str, history: list | None = None, system: str = "You are a helpful assistant.") -> tuple[str, list]:
    messages = (history or []) + [{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": question}]}]
    resp = brt.converse(modelId=MODEL, system=[{"text": system}], messages=messages,
                        inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 1024, "temperature": 0.2})
    msg = resp["output"]["message"]                      # {"role": "assistant", "content": [...]}
    text = "".join(b.get("text", "") for b in msg["content"])
    u = resp["usage"]
    print(f"stop={resp['stopReason']} in={u['inputTokens']} out={u['outputTokens']} "
          f"latency={resp['metrics']['latencyMs']}ms")
    return text, messages + [msg]                        # keep history for the next turn

answer, hist = ask("Explain Iceberg snapshots in two sentences.")
answer, hist = ask("And how do I expire old ones?", hist)  # multi-turn: resend history
print(answer)

Streaming

Stream for any user-facing app so people see text in under a second.

ConverseStreamPython
stream = brt.converse_stream(
    modelId=MODEL,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Write a haiku about S3 lifecycle rules."}]}],
)
for event in stream["stream"]:
    if "contentBlockDelta" in event:
        print(event["contentBlockDelta"]["delta"].get("text", ""), end="", flush=True)
    elif "messageStop" in event:
        print("\nstop:", event["messageStop"]["stopReason"])
    elif "metadata" in event:
        print("usage:", event["metadata"]["usage"])

Documents and images

Ask about a PDF directlyPython
pdf_bytes = open("runbook.pdf", "rb").read()
resp = brt.converse(modelId=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
    {"document": {"format": "pdf", "name": "runbook", "source": {"bytes": pdf_bytes}}},
    {"text": "List every step that needs manual approval."},
]}])

Prompt caching

Put a cachePoint block after content that repeats across calls (long system prompt, tool definitions, a big document). Later calls with the same prefix read it from cache at a fraction of the input price and with lower latency. Check usage.cacheReadInputTokens to confirm it worked. Caching applies only to models that support it and above a minimum prefix length.

Cache a long system promptPython
resp = brt.converse(
    modelId=MODEL,
    system=[{"text": LONG_POLICY_DOC}, {"cachePoint": {"type": "default"}}],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Is a 45-day refund allowed?"}]}],
)
print(resp["usage"].get("cacheReadInputTokens"), resp["usage"].get("cacheWriteInputTokens"))

Errors you'll hit

ErrorMeaningFix
ThrottlingExceptionTokens-per-minute or requests quota hitAdaptive retries with backoff, cross-Region profile, request quota increase, batch inference for offline work
AccessDeniedExceptionIAM missing or model access not enabledCheck role policy for the profile and the underlying model ARNs
ValidationExceptionBad message order, unsupported block, too many tokensMessages must alternate and start with user; check model's limits
ModelTimeoutExceptionLong generationStream, raise read_timeout, lower maxTokens

Calling LLMs on AWS · the most important lesson

Tool use: build the agent loop by hand

Every agent framework is a nicer version of the 40 lines below. Write it yourself once and you will understand LangGraph, Strands, CrewAI and AgentCore harness from the inside, and you'll be able to debug them.

How tool calling works

  1. You send the conversation plus a list of tool specs: name, description, JSON schema for inputs.
  2. The model replies either with text (done) or with one or more toolUse blocks and stopReason = "tool_use".
  3. Your code runs the tool. The model never executes anything itself.
  4. You append the assistant message and a user message containing toolResult blocks with matching toolUseIds.
  5. Call the model again. Repeat until it stops asking for tools, or you hit a limit.
Watch the loop run: "How many Glue jobs failed yesterday and why?"Live lab
    agent_loop.py: a complete tool-using agent with plain boto3Python
    import json, os, boto3

brt = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1")
MODEL = os.environ["BEDROCK_MODEL_ID"]

# 1) Real Python functions are the tools
def list_failed_jobs(date: str) -> list[dict]:
    """Stub: in real life, query the Glue API or your audit Iceberg table."""
    return [{"job": "qm_trusted", "run_id": "jr_1", "error": "OutOfMemory"},
            {"job": "marlo_raw_jp", "run_id": "jr_2", "error": "Timeout calling commercetools"}]

def get_job_log(run_id: str) -> str:
    return {"jr_1": "Container killed: exceeding memory limits", "jr_2": "HTTP 504 after 900s"}[run_id]

TOOLS = {"list_failed_jobs": list_failed_jobs, "get_job_log": get_job_log}

# 2) Describe them to the model (name, description, JSON schema)
TOOL_CONFIG = {"tools": [
    {"toolSpec": {"name": "list_failed_jobs",
                  "description": "List AWS Glue job runs that FAILED on a date (YYYY-MM-DD).",
                  "inputSchema": {"json": {"type": "object",
                                           "properties": {"date": {"type": "string"}},
                                           "required": ["date"]}}}},
    {"toolSpec": {"name": "get_job_log",
                  "description": "Get the error log excerpt for one Glue job run id.",
                  "inputSchema": {"json": {"type": "object",
                                           "properties": {"run_id": {"type": "string"}},
                                           "required": ["run_id"]}}}},
]}

def run_agent(question: str, max_turns: int = 8) -> str:
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": question}]}]
    for turn in range(max_turns):                                   # 3) a hard stop
        resp = brt.converse(modelId=MODEL, messages=messages, toolConfig=TOOL_CONFIG,
                            system=[{"text": "You are an on-call data engineer. Today is 2026-11-03."}],
                            inferenceConfig={"temperature": 0})
        msg = resp["output"]["message"]
        messages.append(msg)                                        # keep the assistant turn
        if resp["stopReason"] != "tool_use":                        # 4) done: final answer
            return "".join(b.get("text", "") for b in msg["content"])
        results = []
        for block in msg["content"]:                                # 5) run every requested tool
            if "toolUse" not in block:
                continue
            call = block["toolUse"]
            try:
                out = TOOLS[call["name"]](**call["input"])
                results.append({"toolResult": {"toolUseId": call["toolUseId"],
                                               "content": [{"json": {"result": out}}]}})
            except Exception as e:                                  # 6) errors go back to the model
                results.append({"toolResult": {"toolUseId": call["toolUseId"], "status": "error",
                                               "content": [{"text": f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"}]}})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})       # 7) observations
    return "Stopped: turn limit reached."

print(run_agent("How many Glue jobs failed yesterday and why?"))

    What you just built

    That loop is ReAct with native tool calling: the model reasons (in its head or in thinking blocks), acts (tool call), observes (tool result), repeats. Everything frameworks add sits around it:

    Line in your loopWhat frameworks add there
    TOOLS and TOOL_CONFIG@tool decorators generate the schema from type hints and docstrings; MCP loads tools from servers
    messages listState objects, checkpointers (resume after crash), memory, summarisation when it gets long
    max_turnsRecursion limits, token budgets, cost limits, timeouts
    Tool executionParallel execution, retries, sandboxes, human approval before risky tools
    The while loop itselfGraphs with branches (LangGraph), multi-agent handoffs (Swarm), hooks/middleware at every step
    printTracing to LangSmith, Langfuse or CloudWatch via OpenTelemetry
    Interview: Does the LLM execute the tool?

    "No. The model only outputs a structured request: tool name and JSON arguments. The application validates and executes it, with its own credentials and permissions, then sends the result back. That's also where security lives: the model can ask for anything, so the tool layer must enforce least privilege, validation and approvals."

    Interview: How do you stop an agent looping forever?

    "Layered stop conditions: a maximum number of turns or tool calls, a token or dollar budget, a wall-clock timeout, and detection of repeated identical tool calls. When a limit hits, return a partial answer with what was done, and log it as an eval failure. In LangGraph that's the recursion limit plus middleware like ModelCallLimit; in Strands, loop limits and hooks; on AgentCore, session limits too."

    Calling LLMs on AWS New 2026

    Mantle and the OpenAI-compatible APIs

    Much GenAI code and many tools are written for the OpenAI SDK. Bedrock now speaks that dialect, so you can reuse that code against Bedrock models by changing two environment variables.

    Point the OpenAI SDK at BedrockTerminal

    List models, then call Chat CompletionsPython
    from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()                       # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY

for m in client.models.list().data:     # what this endpoint serves
    print(m.id)

chat = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="openai.gpt-oss-120b",        # a model id from the list above
    messages=[{"role": "system", "content": "Answer in one sentence."},
              {"role": "user", "content": "What is Apache Iceberg?"}],
)
print(chat.choices[0].message.content)

    Responses API: stateful conversations

    Multi-turn without resending historyPython
    r1 = client.responses.create(model="openai.gpt-oss-120b",
                             input=[{"role": "user", "content": "My table is partitioned by dt. Remember that."}])
r2 = client.responses.create(model="openai.gpt-oss-120b",            # model required on bedrock-runtime
                             previous_response_id=r1.id,             # server rebuilds the context
                             input=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a query for last 7 days."}])
print(r2.output_text)

# Privacy: stored responses are kept 30 days by default. Opt out per call:
client.responses.create(model="openai.gpt-oss-120b", input="hi", store=False)
    Featurebedrock-runtime /openai/v1bedrock-mantle /v1
    Chat CompletionsYesYes
    Responses APIYes, always synchronousYes, plus background=true
    Server-side tools (web search, code interpreter)No (client-side tools only)Yes
    Guardrails on ResponsesNo; use Converse for guardrailed GPT callsSee docs per model
    Projects other than defaultDefault onlyYes
    QuotasShared with Converse/Invoke on that endpointMantle's own quotas
    Why this matters for frameworks

    Anything that accepts an OpenAI-compatible base URL (LangChain's ChatOpenAI, CrewAI via LiteLLM, LlamaIndex OpenAILike, many eval tools) can now use Bedrock models with no AWS-specific provider. LiteLLM and Portkey also list a bedrock_mantle provider.

    Calling LLMs on AWS

    Guardrails, cost and scale

    The features that turn a working call into a production service: content and PII controls, cost control, throughput and offline batch jobs.

    Bedrock Guardrails

    A Guardrail is a reusable policy you attach to a model call (or run standalone with ApplyGuardrail, even on non-Bedrock models). Policies: denied topics, content filters (hate, violence, sexual, misconduct, prompt attack), word filters, sensitive information (PII detect/mask, custom regex), contextual grounding checks (is the answer supported by the source and relevant to the query?) and automated reasoning checks.

    Use a guardrail with Converse, or standalonePython
    resp = brt.converse(modelId=MODEL, messages=msgs,
                    guardrailConfig={"guardrailIdentifier": "gr-abc123", "guardrailVersion": "1", "trace": "enabled"})
if resp["stopReason"] == "guardrail_intervened":
    print("Blocked or masked by guardrail")

# Standalone: check retrieved text or a tool result before the model sees it
chk = brt.apply_guardrail(guardrailIdentifier="gr-abc123", guardrailVersion="1", source="INPUT",
                          content=[{"text": {"text": retrieved_chunk}}])
print(chk["action"])   # NONE | GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED

    Controlling cost

    • Measure first: log input, output, cached and thinking tokens per request and per tenant.
    • Prompt caching for repeated prefixes (system prompts, tools, documents).
    • Model routing: small model for classification and routing, big model only where evals show it's needed.
    • Shorter context: retrieve fewer, better chunks; summarise old turns; drop stale tool outputs.
    • Batch inference (about half the on-demand price) for offline jobs: classify a million support tickets overnight from JSONL in S3.
    • Service tiers / provisioned throughput when you need guaranteed capacity.
    Batch inference job (offline, from S3 JSONL)Python
    bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock")
bedrock.create_model_invocation_job(
    jobName="ticket-classify-2026-11-03",
    roleArn="arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/BedrockBatchRole",
    modelId=MODEL,
    inputDataConfig={"s3InputDataConfig": {"s3Uri": "s3://my-bucket/batch/in/"}},
    outputDataConfig={"s3OutputDataConfig": {"s3Uri": "s3://my-bucket/batch/out/"}},
)
    Data engineer angle

    Batch inference is a Step Functions-friendly, S3-in/S3-out job, exactly like the Glue jobs you already run. "LLM enrichment as a pipeline stage" (classify, extract entities, summarise, embed) is one of the most common Agentic AI Data Engineer tasks.

    Interview: Your GenAI app's bill doubled. How do you investigate?

    "Break cost down by model, feature and tenant from logged token usage, and look at the shape: did request count rise, or tokens per request? Tokens per request usually grows from longer histories, more retrieved chunks, verbose tool outputs left in context, agents taking more turns, or a prompt change that disabled caching. Then fix the biggest bucket: cache stable prefixes, cap and summarise history, trim tool outputs, route easy requests to a small model, set per-run budgets, and move offline work to batch."

    RAG

    Why RAG, and when not to

    Retrieval-Augmented Generation means: before the model answers, fetch the facts it needs from your data and put them in the prompt. It's how you give a model knowledge it was never trained on, keep that knowledge current, and show sources.

    RAG vs long context vs fine-tuning

    NeedBest choice
    Answer from a large, changing, private corpus with citations and per-user permissionsRAG
    Reason over one to a few documents the user just gave youLong context (put them in the prompt, maybe with caching)
    Change style, format, domain vocabulary, or make a small model good at one narrow taskFine-tuning
    Numbers from tables ("revenue by region last month")Text-to-SQL tool, not vector search
    Live state (job status, ticket status)API tool, not an index
    The most common RAG mistake

    Using vector search for structured questions. "How many orders did Japan have yesterday?" needs SQL against a table, not similar-looking paragraphs. Good agents route: documents → retrieval tool, tables → SQL tool, live systems → API tools.

    Where RAG fails (and which lesson fixes it)

    Bad parsing
    Tables flattened, headers lost, scanned PDFs as empty text → parsing and chunking.
    Wrong chunks
    Chunk too big (diluted) or too small (no context) → chunking.
    Vocabulary mismatch
    User says "OOM", docs say "out of memory" → hybrid search, query rewriting.
    Right chunk ranked 9th
    → reranking.
    Multi-hop questions
    → agentic RAG, query decomposition, GraphRAG.
    Stale or deleted documents still retrieved
    → incremental indexing pipeline.
    User sees a document they shouldn't
    → metadata filters with ACLs at query time.
    Answer not supported by the chunks
    → grounding prompts, citations, faithfulness evals.

    RAG · the big picture

    The complete RAG pipeline: every stage and every decision

    Most RAG tutorials show four boxes: split, embed, search, answer. A production system has about fifteen stages, and each one has a decision that changes quality. This lesson is the map. Every later RAG lesson zooms into one part of it, so come back here whenever you lose your place.

    Every stage, its decision, and a safe default

    #StageThe decisionSafe defaultGo deeper
    1LoadWhich sources, full vs incremental, how deletes are detectedEvent-driven incremental load with a manifest tableIndexing pipelines
    2ParsePlain text extraction or layout-aware parsing; OCR; tablesLayout-aware parser for PDFs; tables to MarkdownLoading and parsing
    3CleanRemove boilerplate, de-duplicate, mask PII, detect languageDrop repeated headers/footers; hash-based de-dup; mask before embeddingLoading and parsing, Regulated data
    4ChunkStrategy and sizeStructure-aware, 200–500 tokens, 10–15% overlapChunking, Chunking lab
    5EnrichWhich metadata; contextual prefix; summaries; generated questionsTitle + section path + dates + ACL; contextual prefix if chunks are ambiguousChunking lab
    6EmbedWhich model, dimensions, normalisation, batchingOne general multilingual model, 1,024 dims, normalised; chosen by your own evalEmbedding models
    7IndexWhich store, ANN parameters, keyword index, partitioning by tenantStore you already run; HNSW; a BM25 index next to itVector indexes
    8UnderstandIs retrieval needed at all? Which source? Is the question a follow-up?A cheap router or an agent deciding; standalone rewrite for follow-upsConversational RAG, Agentic RAG
    9TransformRewrite, multi-query, HyDE, decomposition, filter extractionStandalone rewrite + metadata filter extraction; others only if evals show missesQuery transformation
    10RetrieveDense, sparse or both; how many candidatesHybrid, 20–50 candidatesRetrieval strategies
    11Filter + fusePre- or post-filter; fusion methodACL and metadata pre-filter; RRF with k = 60Advanced retrieval
    12RerankReranker model, how many to keep, score thresholdCross-encoder reranker, keep 3–8, refuse below a calibrated thresholdAdvanced retrieval
    13PackToken budget, order, de-dup, compression, parent expansionBest first, de-dup by document, fit a fixed budgetContext and generation
    14GeneratePrompt, model, citations format, refusal rule"Only from sources, cite [n], say I don't know"; temperature 0Context and generation
    15Verify + logGrounding check, citation check, what to traceProgrammatic citation check; sampled judge; full trace with chunk IDsRAG eval lab

    Four maturity levels

    Naive RAG
    Fixed-size chunks, one vector search, top-k into the prompt. Works for demos; fails on exact identifiers, follow-ups and multi-part questions.
    Advanced RAG
    Adds better parsing and chunking, hybrid search, reranking, query rewriting and metadata filters. This is the level most production systems should reach first.
    Modular RAG
    Stages become swappable components chosen per question by a router: different indexes, SQL for tables, a web tool for fresh facts.
    Agentic RAG
    An agent decides whether, where and how often to retrieve, grades what it finds and retries. Most capable, most expensive, needs budgets and trajectory evals.
    How to improve a RAG system, in order

    1. Build an eval set and measure recall@k and faithfulness. 2. Fix parsing and chunking. 3. Add hybrid search and a reranker. 4. Add query rewriting and filters. 5. Only then consider agentic loops, GraphRAG or fine-tuned embeddings. Each step is measured against the same eval set. Most teams that skip step 1 end up changing models instead of fixing their data.

    Interview: Draw the architecture of a production RAG system and explain each stage.

    "There are two pipelines joined by the index. Offline, documents are loaded incrementally from their sources, parsed with a layout-aware parser so tables and headings survive, cleaned and de-duplicated, masked for PII, split into structure-aware chunks of a few hundred tokens, enriched with metadata such as title, section, dates and access groups, embedded, and written to a vector index with a keyword index alongside. Online, the question is first understood: is it a follow-up, does it need retrieval, which source? It's rewritten into a standalone query, filters are extracted, hybrid retrieval fetches 20 to 50 candidates within the caller's permissions, results are fused with reciprocal rank fusion and reranked by a cross-encoder down to a handful, packed into a fixed token budget, and the model answers only from them with citations or says it doesn't know. Finally the answer is checked for grounding and every step is traced with chunk IDs so it can be evaluated and debugged."

    RAG

    Embeddings and vector search

    An embedding model turns text into a list of numbers (say 1,024) so that texts with similar meaning have vectors pointing in similar directions. Search becomes "find the nearest vectors".

    Cosine similarity, visualised in 2DLive lab

    Pick a query. Real embeddings have ~1,000 dimensions; these 2D points are a hand-made projection to show the idea.

    Similarity measures

    Cosine similarity
    cos θ = (a·b)/(|a||b|). 1 = same direction, 0 = unrelated. Default for text.
    Dot product
    Same as cosine when vectors are normalised (most embedding APIs can normalise for you).
    Euclidean (L2)
    Straight-line distance. Used by some indexes; equivalent ranking for normalised vectors.
    Embed with Titan Text Embeddings V2 and comparePython
    import json, boto3, numpy as np
brt = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1")

def embed(text: str, dims: int = 1024) -> np.ndarray:
    body = {"inputText": text, "dimensions": dims, "normalize": True}
    r = brt.invoke_model(modelId="amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0", body=json.dumps(body))
    return np.array(json.loads(r["body"].read())["embedding"])

q = embed("Glue job ran out of memory")
docs = ["Executor OOM: increase worker type to G.2X", "How to rotate IAM access keys", "Spark container killed: memory overhead exceeded"]
vecs = np.stack([embed(d) for d in docs])
scores = vecs @ q                        # normalised, so dot product = cosine
for d, s in sorted(zip(docs, scores), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
    print(f"{s:.3f}  {d}")

    Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN)

    Comparing a query against 50 million vectors one by one is too slow. Vector indexes use ANN algorithms that trade a little recall for huge speed:

    HNSW
    A layered graph of neighbours; search hops from coarse to fine layers. Fast, high recall, memory-hungry. Default in OpenSearch, pgvector, most vector DBs. Tune m, ef_construction, ef_search.
    IVF
    Cluster vectors; search only the nearest clusters. Lower memory; tune number of lists and probes.
    Quantisation (PQ, binary, int8)
    Compress vectors to cut memory and cost, with a small accuracy loss; often re-score the top results with full vectors.

    Vector stores on and around AWS

    StoreGood forNotes
    Amazon S3 VectorsLarge, cost-sensitive corpora; infrequent queriesVector buckets and indexes inside S3; sub-second queries; very low storage cost; Bedrock Knowledge Bases integration
    OpenSearch Service / ServerlessHybrid search (BM25 + vectors), filters, high QPSMost flexible on AWS; you tune shards and HNSW
    Aurora PostgreSQL / RDS with pgvectorVectors next to relational data, SQL filters and joinsGreat when your metadata is already in Postgres; HNSW and IVFFlat indexes
    Bedrock Managed Knowledge BaseManaged end-to-end RAGNo vector store to run; built-in agentic multi-hop retrieval (GA June 2026)
    Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, MongoDB AtlasSpecialised or multi-cloudSupported as Knowledge Base or framework backends
    FAISS, ChromaLocal prototyping and testsIn-process; not a production service by themselves
    Interview: How do you choose an embedding model and dimension?

    "Run a retrieval eval on my own data: 50 to 200 real questions labelled with the chunks that answer them, and compare recall@k and MRR across two or three models. Check language coverage, max input length and cost. Bigger dimensions can help slightly but cost storage and latency; many models support smaller output dimensions with little loss, so I'd test 1024 vs 512. And I keep the model ID with every vector, because changing models means re-embedding everything; you can't mix vectors from different models."

    RAG · fundamentals + hands-on

    Embedding models: choosing, using and tuning

    The embedding model decides what "similar" means for your whole system. Switching it later means re-embedding everything, so choose with care: on your own data, with a measurement, considering dimensions, languages, cost and the tricks that make vectors smaller.

    What to compare

    PropertyWhy it matters
    Retrieval quality on your questionsPublic leaderboards (MTEB) are a starting shortlist, not an answer; domain text, abbreviations and IDs behave differently
    LanguagesEnglish-only models degrade badly on Japanese, Italian or Telugu; cross-lingual search needs a multilingual model
    Max input tokensText beyond the limit is truncated silently or rejected; it caps your chunk size
    Dimensions and flexible sizesStorage, memory and search speed scale with dimensions; some models let you choose smaller sizes
    Query vs document input typesAsymmetric models embed questions and passages differently; using the wrong type hurts recall
    ModalitiesText only, or text + images (+ video/audio) in one vector space
    Output typesfloat, int8 or binary vectors; smaller types cut cost
    Price and throughputRe-indexing 50 million chunks must be affordable and fit quotas

    Embedding models on Bedrock (verify IDs and options in your Region)

    ModelNotes
    Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 (amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0)Text; 1,024, 512 or 256 dimensions; optional normalisation; up to 8k tokens; multilingual support
    Cohere Embed (English and Multilingual v3, and Embed v4)Asymmetric: pass input_type (search_document or search_query); multilingual; Embed v4 adds images, choosable output dimensions and int8/binary output types
    Amazon Nova multimodal embeddingsOne vector space for text, images, documents, video and audio; several dimension sizes
    Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1Older text + image model
    Calling the two common families (bodies differ per model: check the model card)Python
    import json, boto3
brt = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1")

def titan_v2(texts: list[str], dims: int = 1024) -> list[list[float]]:
    out = []
    for t in texts:                                           # Titan V2 takes one text per call
        r = brt.invoke_model(modelId="amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0",
                             body=json.dumps({"inputText": t, "dimensions": dims, "normalize": True}))
        out.append(json.loads(r["body"].read())["embedding"])
    return out

def cohere(texts: list[str], kind: str, model_id: str = "cohere.embed-multilingual-v3") -> list[list[float]]:
    """kind = 'search_document' when indexing, 'search_query' when searching. Cohere accepts a batch of texts."""
    r = brt.invoke_model(modelId=model_id, body=json.dumps(
        {"texts": texts, "input_type": kind, "truncate": "END"}))
    body = json.loads(r["body"].read())
    return body["embeddings"]           # with embedding_types=["float"] this becomes body["embeddings"]["float"]

# doc_vecs   = cohere(chunks, "search_document")
# query_vec  = cohere([question], "search_query")[0]
    The two mistakes that silently ruin retrieval

    1. Mixing models or settings. Vectors from different models, different dimension settings, or normalised vs un-normalised, are not comparable. Store the model ID and settings with every vector and never mix them in one index. 2. Wrong input type. With asymmetric models, documents indexed as search_query (or the reverse) lose noticeable recall with no error message.

    Making vectors cheaper: dimensions and quantisation

    A float32 vector of 1,024 dimensions is 4 KB. Fifty million of them is 200 GB before index overhead. Three tricks shrink that:

    Smaller dimensions
    Models trained with Matryoshka representation learning put the most important information in the first dimensions, so you can keep the first 256 or 512 and re-normalise. Only do this with models that support it (the model offers a dimensions option).
    int8 quantisation
    Store each dimension in one byte instead of four: 4× smaller, usually tiny recall loss.
    Binary quantisation
    Store only the sign of each dimension: 32× smaller and very fast Hamming distance. Recall drops, so use it to fetch candidates and rescore the top ones with full vectors.
    quantize.py: binary search + rescoring keeps recall while cutting memory 32x (NumPy only)Python
    import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

# 20,000 synthetic "document embeddings" with cluster structure, normalised like a real model's output
dims = 512
centers = rng.normal(size=(500, dims))
docs = centers[rng.integers(0, 500, 20_000)] + 0.5 * rng.normal(size=(20_000, dims))
docs /= np.linalg.norm(docs, axis=1, keepdims=True)
queries = docs[rng.integers(0, 20_000, 100)] + 0.5 * rng.normal(size=(100, dims)) / np.sqrt(dims)
queries /= np.linalg.norm(queries, axis=1, keepdims=True)

def topk(scores, k):
    return np.argsort(-scores, axis=1)[:, :k]

truth = topk(queries @ docs.T, 10)                               # exact float search = ground truth

bits_d, bits_q = (docs > 0).astype(np.float32), (queries > 0).astype(np.float32)   # 1 bit per dimension
agree = bits_q @ bits_d.T + (1 - bits_q) @ (1 - bits_d).T        # bits that match = dims - Hamming distance
binary_only = topk(agree, 10)

cand = topk(agree, 100)                                          # binary: cheap candidate fetch
rescored = np.array([c[np.argsort(-(docs[c] @ q))[:10]] for c, q in zip(cand, queries)])  # float rescore

recall = lambda got: np.mean([len(set(g) & set(t)) / 10 for g, t in zip(got, truth)])
print(f"float32 index size: {docs.astype(np.float32).nbytes / 1e6:.1f} MB | binary: {np.packbits(bits_d > 0, axis=1).nbytes / 1e6:.2f} MB")
print(f"recall@10 binary only:          {recall(binary_only):.2f}")
print(f"recall@10 binary + rescore 100: {recall(rescored):.2f}")
    OutputOutput
    float32 index size: 41.0 MB | binary: 1.28 MB
recall@10 binary only:          0.47
recall@10 binary + rescore 100: 1.00

    Dense, sparse and late-interaction

    KindRepresentationStrengthWeakness
    Dense (bi-encoder)One vector per chunkMeaning, paraphrases, cross-lingualExact tokens, rare IDs
    Sparse lexical (BM25)Term weights over the vocabularyExact terms, codes, names; no trainingSynonyms, paraphrase
    Learned sparse (e.g. SPLADE)Model-weighted terms, including expansionsExact terms plus some semanticsNeeds supporting store and model
    Late interaction (ColBERT-style)One vector per tokenVery high quality matchingMuch more storage; specialised engines

    The practical 2026 default is dense + BM25 fused with RRF, then a cross-encoder reranker. That covers most of what the more exotic options offer.

    Choosing with your own evaluation

    Compare embedding models on your labelled questions (plug in real embed functions)Python
    import numpy as np

def recall_at_k(embed_docs, embed_query, chunks: dict[str, str], gold: list[tuple[str, str]], k: int = 5) -> float:
    ids = list(chunks)
    D = np.array(embed_docs([chunks[i] for i in ids]), dtype=float)
    D /= np.linalg.norm(D, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    hits = 0
    for question, expected_id in gold:
        q = np.array(embed_query(question), dtype=float); q /= np.linalg.norm(q)
        top = [ids[j] for j in np.argsort(-(D @ q))[:k]]
        hits += expected_id in top
    return hits / len(gold)

# for name, (ed, eq) in {"titan-1024": (lambda t: titan_v2(t, 1024), lambda q: titan_v2([q])[0]),
#                        "cohere-multi": (lambda t: cohere(t, "search_document"), lambda q: cohere([q], "search_query")[0])}.items():
#     print(name, recall_at_k(ed, eq, chunks, gold))

    Fine-tuning an embedding model

    Worth considering when your domain vocabulary is unusual (internal product codes, clinical shorthand) and recall plateaus after hybrid search and reranking. You need a few thousand (question, relevant passage) pairs: from search logs, from support tickets, or generated by an LLM from your documents and then reviewed. A typical recipe is an open embedding model fine-tuned with a contrastive loss (in-batch negatives), served from SageMaker. Re-embedding the corpus is part of the cost, and you must re-run the same retrieval eval to prove it helped.

    Interview: How would you choose an embedding model for a multilingual enterprise RAG?

    "I'd shortlist two or three multilingual models available in our Region, for example Cohere's multilingual model and Titan V2, then build a labelled set of real questions in each language with the passages that answer them, including cross-lingual cases if questions and documents can be in different languages. I'd index the same chunks with each model and compare recall@5 per language, plus latency, cost per million tokens and vector size. I'd check practical constraints: max input tokens versus my chunk size, query versus document input types, and whether smaller dimensions or int8 output are supported to reduce storage. I'd store the model ID with every vector so a future switch is a clean rebuild."

    Interview: Your vector index is too expensive at 50 million chunks. What can you do without losing much quality?

    "First, use fewer dimensions if the model supports flexible sizes, such as 512 instead of 1,024. Second, quantise: int8 is four times smaller with little loss, and binary is 32 times smaller if I fetch candidates with binary vectors and rescore the top hundred with full-precision vectors, which recovers most of the recall. Third, tier the storage: hot tenants in an in-memory index, cold ones in a cheaper store such as S3 Vectors. And check the corpus itself: de-duplicate near-identical chunks and drop boilerplate. I'd measure recall@10 against exact search before and after each change."

    RAG · fundamentals

    Vector indexes and choosing a store on AWS

    An embedding search is "find the nearest vectors to this one". Doing that exactly over millions of vectors is too slow, so vector databases use approximate indexes. Knowing how HNSW and IVF work, and which AWS store fits which workload, is a standard interview topic.

    Exact vs approximate search

    Exact (flat, brute force)
    Compare the query with every vector. Perfect recall, cost grows linearly. Fine up to roughly a few hundred thousand vectors, and the right baseline for measuring other indexes.
    Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN)
    Build an index that looks at a small part of the data. You trade a little recall (say 95–99% of the true neighbours) for a 10–1000× speed-up.

    HNSW: the default index

    Hierarchical Navigable Small World builds a layered graph. Each vector is a node linked to its nearest neighbours. Upper layers are sparse "motorways", the bottom layer contains every vector. A search enters at the top, greedily hops toward the query, drops a layer, and repeats.

    ParameterMeaningRaise it to getCost
    MLinks per nodeBetter recallMore memory, slower build
    ef_constructionCandidates considered while buildingBetter graph qualitySlower indexing
    ef_searchCandidates considered per queryBetter recall at query timeHigher latency (tunable per query)

    The other names you'll hear

    IVF (inverted file)
    Cluster vectors with k-means into nlist buckets; at query time search only the nprobe nearest buckets. Less memory than HNSW, faster to build, lower recall at the same speed. Needs training data and re-clustering as data drifts.
    PQ (product quantisation)
    Compress each vector into a few bytes by splitting it into sub-vectors and storing the nearest codebook entry for each. Big memory savings, some recall loss. Often combined: IVF-PQ.
    Scalar / binary quantisation
    Store each dimension as 8 bits or 1 bit instead of a 32-bit float. 4–32× smaller; rescore the top candidates with full vectors to recover accuracy.
    Disk-based ANN
    Indexes designed to keep most data on SSD or object storage instead of RAM. Cheaper at very large scale, slower per query. S3 Vectors sits in this cost-first corner.
    Pre-filter vs post-filter
    Applying a metadata filter before the vector search guarantees k results but needs index support; filtering after is simple but may return fewer than k when the filter is selective.

    Distance metrics

    Cosine similarity compares direction and ignores length; dot product equals cosine when vectors are normalised to length 1 (most embedding APIs can normalise for you); Euclidean (L2) measures straight-line distance. Use the metric the embedding model was trained with, which is nearly always cosine or dot product. Index and query must use the same metric.

    Choosing a vector store on AWS

    StoreGood atWatch out forPick it when
    Aurora / RDS PostgreSQL + pgvectorVectors next to relational data, SQL filters and joins, transactions, full-text search for hybrid in one queryYou tune and scale the database; very large indexes need memoryYou already run Postgres, up to tens of millions of vectors, and want one system
    OpenSearch (Serverless or managed)Native hybrid search (BM25 + k-NN), rich filtering, large scale, several ANN enginesCost floor for always-on capacity; more to operateSearch-heavy products, high QPS, hybrid is a must
    S3 VectorsVery low storage cost, no servers, huge volumesHigher latency and lower QPS than in-memory indexes; fewer query featuresLarge, infrequently queried corpora; archives; cost-first agents
    Bedrock Knowledge BasesManaged ingestion, chunking, embedding, sync and retrieval API on top of the stores aboveLess control over each stepStandard document RAG you don't want to hand-build
    Neptune AnalyticsGraph + vector for GraphRAGOnly worth it when relationships matterMulti-hop questions across linked entities
    MemoryDB / ElastiCache (Valkey)Single-digit-millisecond vector search in memoryRAM costSemantic caches and real-time lookups
    How to answer "which vector DB?"

    Don't name a favourite. Ask four things: how many vectors, what query rate and latency, what filters and hybrid needs, and what the team already runs. Then pick the simplest store that meets them, and say you'd measure recall@k against exact search before trusting any ANN setting.

    Interview: Explain HNSW and how you'd tune it.

    "HNSW is a multi-layer proximity graph. Higher layers have few nodes with long-range links, the bottom layer has every vector. Search starts at the top, greedily moves to the neighbour closest to the query, then descends and refines. M controls links per node, ef_construction controls build quality, and ef_search controls how many candidates each query explores. To tune it I build a ground-truth set with exact search on a sample, then raise ef_search until recall@k is around 95–99% and check p95 latency. If recall is still poor I rebuild with higher M or ef_construction. Memory is the main cost, so at large scale I'd add quantisation and rescoring."

    Interview: Your filtered vector search returns 2 results when you asked for 10. Why?

    "That's post-filtering: the index returned its top k nearest vectors, then the metadata filter removed most of them. Fixes are to use a store or index that filters during the search, to over-fetch and then filter, or to partition the index by the filter key, for example one index or namespace per tenant. In pgvector I'd also check the query plan, because with a selective WHERE clause the planner may be better off using the B-tree index and exact distance."

    RAG · hands-on

    Loading and parsing documents

    "Garbage in, garbage out" is truer for RAG than for any pipeline you have built. If a table is flattened into a line of numbers, or a page header is repeated into every chunk, no embedding model or reranker can recover it. Parsing is where most retrieval quality is won or lost.

    What each source needs

    SourceProblemWhat to use
    Digital PDF (text layer)Reading order across columns; headers, footers, page numbers; tables become word soupLayout-aware parser (Docling, Unstructured, PyMuPDF with layout); Textract LAYOUT + TABLES
    Scanned PDF / imagesNo text at allOCR: Amazon Textract; Bedrock Data Automation; a multimodal model for complex pages
    Word, PowerPointStyles carry structure (Heading 1, bullet levels); speaker notespython-docx / python-pptx, or Unstructured; keep headings as Markdown
    HTML, Confluence, wikisNavigation, menus, cookie banners, macrosExtract the main content element; keep h1–h3 as section path; Knowledge Base connectors
    Spreadsheets, CSVRows have no meaning without headersRow-to-text with headers repeated, or load into a table and use text-to-SQL
    Email, ticketsQuoted replies and signatures repeatStrip quoted history and signatures; keep subject, author, date as metadata
    CodeSplitting mid-function breaks meaningLanguage-aware splitting by function/class; include file path and symbol name

    Parsing options on AWS

    Amazon Textract
    OCR plus structure: AnalyzeDocument with feature types TABLES, FORMS, LAYOUT, QUERIES. Synchronous for single pages, asynchronous (StartDocumentAnalysis) for multi-page PDFs in S3.
    Bedrock Data Automation
    Managed extraction of text, tables, figures and custom fields from documents, images, audio and video, with output you can feed to an index.
    Knowledge Bases parsing options
    Default text parsing, a foundation-model parser (a multimodal model reads each page, good for tables and figures), or Bedrock Data Automation as the parser.
    Open source
    Docling and Unstructured for layout-aware conversion to Markdown/JSON; pypdf or PyMuPDF for quick text; LlamaParse as a hosted option.

    Turn HTML into sections with a heading path (standard library only)

    html_sections.py: keep headings as structure, drop navigation, emit one record per sectionPython
    from html.parser import HTMLParser

class Sectioner(HTMLParser):
    SKIP = {"nav", "footer", "header", "script", "style", "aside"}
    HEADINGS = {"h1": 1, "h2": 2, "h3": 3}

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.path, self.sections, self.buf, self.skip_depth, self.in_heading = [], [], [], 0, None

    def flush(self):
        text = " ".join(" ".join(self.buf).split())
        if text:
            self.sections.append({"section": " > ".join(self.path) or "(intro)", "text": text})
        self.buf = []

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        if tag in self.SKIP:
            self.skip_depth += 1
        elif tag in self.HEADINGS and not self.skip_depth:
            self.flush()
            self.in_heading, self.heading_text = tag, []

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag in self.SKIP and self.skip_depth:
            self.skip_depth -= 1
        elif tag == self.in_heading:
            level = self.HEADINGS[tag]
            self.path = self.path[: level - 1] + [" ".join(self.heading_text).strip()]
            self.in_heading = None

    def handle_data(self, data):
        if self.skip_depth:
            return
        (self.heading_text if self.in_heading else self.buf).append(data)

page = """<html><body><nav>Home | Runbooks | Login</nav>
<h1>Quantum pipeline runbook</h1><p>Owner: data platform team.</p>
<h2>Failures</h2><h3>Out of memory</h3><p>Move workers from G.1X to G.2X. Avoid collect().</p>
<h3>Missing watermark</h3><p>The job falls back to a full load.</p>
<footer>(c) 2026 Example Corp</footer></body></html>"""

for s in p.sections:

Quantum pipeline runbook > Failures > Out of memory | Move workers from G.1X to G.2X. Avoid collect().
Quantum pipeline runbook > Failures > Missing watermark | The job falls back to a full load.

    The heading path ("Quantum pipeline runbook > Failures > Out of memory") becomes metadata and, often, a prefix of the chunk text. A chunk that says "Move workers to G.2X" means much more when the embedding also sees which runbook and which failure it belongs to.

    Tables: keep the header with every row

    table_to_text.py: two table formats that survive chunkingPython
    rows = [["job", "worker", "avg_minutes", "owner"],
        ["qm_trusted_load", "G.2X", "27", "data-platform"],
        ["marlo_enriched", "G.1X", "9", "commerce-data"]]

def as_markdown(rows):
    head, *body = rows
    lines = ["| " + " | ".join(head) + " |", "|" + "---|" * len(head)]
    return "\n".join(lines + ["| " + " | ".join(r) + " |" for r in body])

def as_row_sentences(rows, table_name):
    head, *body = rows
    return [f"{table_name}: " + "; ".join(f"{h} = {v}" for h, v in zip(head, r)) for r in body]

print(as_markdown(rows))
print()
for line in as_row_sentences(rows, "Glue job catalogue"):
    print(line)
    OutputOutput
    | job | worker | avg_minutes | owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| qm_trusted_load | G.2X | 27 | data-platform |
| marlo_enriched | G.1X | 9 | commerce-data |

Glue job catalogue: job = qm_trusted_load; worker = G.2X; avg_minutes = 27; owner = data-platform
Glue job catalogue: job = marlo_enriched; worker = G.1X; avg_minutes = 9; owner = commerce-data

    Use Markdown when the table is small enough to stay in one chunk. Use one sentence per row (with headers repeated) for long tables, so any chunk boundary still leaves each row self-explanatory. If people mostly ask aggregate questions about the table ("which jobs average over 20 minutes?"), load it into a real table and use text-to-SQL instead.

    Cleaning rules that pay off

    clean.py: remove repeated page furniture, fix hyphenation, normalise whitespacePython
    import re
from collections import Counter

def clean_pages(pages: list[str], min_repeat_ratio: float = 0.6) -> list[str]:
    """Lines that appear on most pages (headers, footers, 'Confidential') are furniture, not content."""
    counts = Counter(line.strip() for p in pages for line in set(p.splitlines()) if line.strip())
    furniture = {line for line, n in counts.items() if n / len(pages) >= min_repeat_ratio}
    out = []
    for p in pages:
        lines = [l for l in p.splitlines() if l.strip() and l.strip() not in furniture]
        text = "\n".join(lines)
        text = re.sub(r"(\w)-\n(\w)", r"\1\2", text)          # re-join words hyphenated across lines
        text = re.sub(r"(?<!\n)\n(?!\n)", " ", text)           # single newlines inside paragraphs -> spaces
        text = re.sub(r"[ \t]+", " ", text).strip()
        out.append(text)
    return out

pages = ["ACME Data Platform - Confidential\nIncremental loads read the water-\nmark from DynamoDB.\nPage 1",
         "ACME Data Platform - Confidential\nIf the watermark is missing the job\nruns a full load.\nPage 2",
         "ACME Data Platform - Confidential\nBackdated files are stored separately.\nPage 3"]
for p in clean_pages(pages):
    print(repr(p))
    OutputOutput
    'Incremental loads read the watermark from DynamoDB. Page 1'
'If the watermark is missing the job runs a full load. Page 2'
'Backdated files are stored separately. Page 3'
    "Page 1", "Page 2" survived

    Page numbers differ on every page, so frequency-based removal misses them. Add explicit patterns for the furniture you see in your corpus (page numbers, document IDs, dates in footers). Open twenty random parsed documents and read them before you tune anything else. It is the cheapest RAG improvement there is.

    Interview: A user says the bot never answers questions about tables in our PDFs. How do you fix it?

    "I'd look at the parsed output first, because the usual cause is that tables were extracted as a stream of numbers without headers, so neither embeddings nor the model can use them. I'd switch to a layout-aware parser or Textract with the TABLES feature, convert each table to Markdown if it's small or to one sentence per row with headers repeated if it's large, and keep table and section titles as metadata. I'd also add a short generated description of each table for retrieval. Then I'd add table questions to the eval set and compare recall before and after. If users mostly ask aggregate questions over the tables, I'd load them into a real table and route those questions to text-to-SQL."

    RAG

    Parsing and chunking

    Retrieval quality is mostly decided before any vector is created: how well you extract text from source files and how you cut it into chunks. Try the chunker below with your own text.

    Chunking playgroundLive lab

    Chunking strategies

    StrategyHowWhen
    Fixed size + overlapN tokens with 10–20% overlapBaseline; uniform text
    Recursive / structure-awareSplit on headings, then paragraphs, then sentences until under the sizeMost documents (LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter, Markdown/HTML splitters)
    SemanticSplit where embedding similarity between sentences dropsLong, topic-shifting text
    Hierarchical (parent-child)Search small child chunks; return their larger parent sectionNeed precise matching and enough context to answer
    Contextual chunksPrepend an LLM-written sentence situating each chunk in its document before embeddingWhen chunks are ambiguous out of context ("it", "this table")
    Late chunkingEmbed the whole document with a long-context embedder, then pool token vectors per chunkKeeps document context in each chunk vector; needs supporting models
    Code / tablesSplit by function or class; keep table rows with headers; convert tables to MarkdownRepos, specs, spreadsheets

    Metadata is half the value

    Store with every chunk: doc_id, source_uri, title, section path, updated_at, version, content hash, acl (groups allowed), doc_type, region/business unit, embedding model ID. You'll filter on it ("only Japan docs this user can see, updated this year"), show it as citations, and use it to update and delete.

    Structure-aware chunks with metadata (LangChain splitters)Python
    from langchain_text_splitters import MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter, RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
import hashlib

md = open("runbook.md").read()
sections = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter(headers_to_split_on=[("#", "h1"), ("##", "h2")]).split_text(md)
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1200, chunk_overlap=150)   # characters

chunks = []
for sec in sections:
    for i, piece in enumerate(splitter.split_text(sec.page_content)):
        heading = " > ".join(v for v in sec.metadata.values())
        chunks.append({
            "text": f"{heading}\n\n{piece}",            # heading text helps both embedding and the LLM
            "metadata": {**sec.metadata, "doc_id": "runbook", "chunk": i,
                         "sha": hashlib.sha256(piece.encode()).hexdigest()[:16],
                         "acl": ["data-eng"], "source_uri": "s3://kb/runbook.md"},
        })
print(len(chunks), chunks[0]["text"][:120])

    Parsing tools

    Amazon Textract (scanned PDFs, forms, tables), Bedrock Data Automation and Knowledge Bases' advanced parsing (foundation-model parsing of complex PDFs), LlamaParse, Unstructured, Docling, PyMuPDF for born-digital PDFs. For images and diagrams in documents, multimodal models can produce text descriptions to index.

    Interview: What chunk size do you use?

    "There's no universal number; I start around 300–800 tokens with 10–15% overlap, split on document structure, and then tune using a retrieval eval. Smaller chunks give precise matches but lose context; larger ones carry context but dilute the embedding and waste prompt tokens. If I need both, I use parent-child: search small chunks, return the parent section. I also add the document title and heading path to every chunk."

    RAG · hands-on

    Chunking lab: six strategies with code

    The previous lesson listed chunking strategies. Here you implement each one in plain Python, so you know exactly what a library does when you call it, and you can explain the trade-offs from first principles in an interview. Every snippet runs without any API.

    1. Recursive splitting (what most libraries do by default)

    Try to split on the biggest natural boundary first (blank lines), and only fall back to smaller ones (newlines, sentences, spaces) for pieces that are still too long. Then merge small neighbours back up to the size limit.

    recursive.pyPython
    SEPARATORS = ["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " "]

def split_recursive(text: str, max_chars: int, seps=SEPARATORS) -> list[str]:
    if len(text) <= max_chars:
        return [text]
    if not seps:                                        # nothing left to split on: hard cut
        return [text[i:i + max_chars] for i in range(0, len(text), max_chars)]
    sep, rest = seps[0], seps[1:]
    if sep not in text:                                 # this separator isn't present: try a smaller one
        return split_recursive(text, max_chars, rest)
    parts = text.split(sep)
    parts = [p + sep if i < len(parts) - 1 else p for i, p in enumerate(parts)]   # keep the separator
    chunks, cur = [], ""
    for p in parts:
        if len(p) > max_chars:                          # still too big: recurse with smaller separators
            if cur:
                chunks.append(cur); cur = ""
            chunks += split_recursive(p, max_chars, rest)
        elif len(cur) + len(p) <= max_chars:            # merge small neighbours up to the limit
            cur += p
        else:
            chunks.append(cur); cur = p
    if cur:
        chunks.append(cur)
    return [c.strip() for c in chunks if c.strip()]

doc = """Incremental loads. The job reads the last watermark from DynamoDB. It loads only newer files.

Fallback. If the watermark is missing, the job runs a full load. This is slower but safe.

Backdated files. Files with an older event date are stored in a separate prefix and reprocessed weekly."""
for c in split_recursive(doc, 80):
    print(len(c), "|", c.replace("\n", " "))

    2. Structure-aware with a heading breadcrumb

    markdown_chunks.py: split by headings, prefix each chunk with its pathPython
    def markdown_chunks(md: str, title: str) -> list[dict]:
    path, chunks, body = [], [], []
    def emit():
        text = " ".join(" ".join(body).split())
        if text:
            crumb = " > ".join([title] + path)
            chunks.append({"section": crumb, "text": f"[{crumb}] {text}"})
    for line in md.splitlines():
        if line.startswith("#"):
            emit(); body.clear()
            level = len(line) - len(line.lstrip("#"))
            path[:] = path[: level - 1] + [line.lstrip("# ").strip()]
        else:
            body.append(line)
    emit()
    return chunks

md = """# Failures
## Out of memory
Move workers from G.1X to G.2X.
## Missing watermark
The job falls back to a full load.
# Maintenance
Expire Iceberg snapshots weekly."""
for c in markdown_chunks(md, "Quantum runbook"):
    print(c["text"])
    OutputOutput
    [Quantum runbook > Failures > Out of memory] Move workers from G.1X to G.2X.
[Quantum runbook > Failures > Missing watermark] The job falls back to a full load.
[Quantum runbook > Maintenance] Expire Iceberg snapshots weekly.

    The breadcrumb is embedded with the text, so a question about "the Quantum runbook's memory errors" can match a chunk that itself only says "Move workers…". This one change often beats switching embedding models.

    3. Semantic chunking: cut where the topic changes

    Embed each sentence, measure similarity between neighbours, and start a new chunk where similarity drops sharply. The demo uses a tiny bag-of-words "embedding" so it runs offline; with a real embedding model the logic is identical.

    semantic.pyPython
    import re
import numpy as np

def toy_embed(s: str, vocab: list[str]) -> np.ndarray:          # replace with a real embedding model
    words = re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", s.lower())
    v = np.array([sum(w.startswith(t) for w in words) for t in vocab], dtype=float)
    return v / (np.linalg.norm(v) or 1)

def semantic_chunks(text: str, vocab: list[str], percentile: float = 80) -> list[str]:
    sents = [s.strip() for s in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", text) if s.strip()]
    vecs = np.array([toy_embed(s, vocab) for s in sents])
    sims = (vecs[:-1] * vecs[1:]).sum(axis=1)                    # similarity of each sentence to the next
    distance = 1 - sims
    cut = np.percentile(distance, percentile)                    # breakpoints = the largest jumps
    chunks, cur = [], [sents[0]]
    for i, d in enumerate(distance):
        if d > cut:
            chunks.append(" ".join(cur)); cur = []
        cur.append(sents[i + 1])
    return chunks + [" ".join(cur)]

text = ("Glue workers ran out of memory. Memory errors happen on G.1X workers. "
        "Move memory-heavy jobs to G.2X workers. "
        "Iceberg tables need snapshot expiry. Old Iceberg snapshots waste storage. "
        "Snapshot expiry runs weekly.")
vocab = ["glue", "memory", "worker", "g", "iceberg", "snapshot", "expir", "storage"]
for c in semantic_chunks(text, vocab):
    print("-", c)
    OutputOutput
    - Glue workers ran out of memory. Memory errors happen on G.1X workers. Move memory-heavy jobs to G.2X workers.
- Iceberg tables need snapshot expiry. Old Iceberg snapshots waste storage. Snapshot expiry runs weekly.
    When semantic chunking is worth it

    Long, unstructured text that drifts between topics (transcripts, meeting notes, long emails). For documents with real headings, structure-aware splitting is cheaper and usually as good. Semantic chunking costs one embedding per sentence at index time and produces uneven chunk sizes, so cap the maximum size as well.

    4. Parent–child (small-to-big)

    Small chunks retrieve precisely; big chunks answer completely. Index the children, return the parent.

    parent_child.pyPython
    def parent_child(sections: list[dict], child_chars: int = 60) -> tuple[dict, list[dict]]:
    parents, children = {}, []
    for i, s in enumerate(sections):
        pid = f"p{i}"
        parents[pid] = s["text"]
        words, cur = s["text"].split(), ""
        for w in words:
            if len(cur) + len(w) + 1 > child_chars:
                children.append({"id": f"{pid}.c{len(children)}", "parent": pid, "text": cur.strip()}); cur = ""
            cur += " " + w
        if cur.strip():
            children.append({"id": f"{pid}.c{len(children)}", "parent": pid, "text": cur.strip()})
    return parents, children

sections = [{"text": "Out of memory on Glue: move workers from G.1X to G.2X, avoid collect() on large DataFrames, "
                     "and check for skewed join keys before adding workers."},
            {"text": "Missing watermark: the job falls back to a full load, which takes about 30 minutes for 100 GB."}]
parents, children = parent_child(sections)
for c in children:
    print(c["id"], "->", c["text"])
hit = "p0.c1"                                         # pretend vector search matched this child
pid = next(c["parent"] for c in children if c["id"] == hit)
print("\nsend to the LLM:", parents[pid])
    OutputOutput
    p0.c0 -> Out of memory on Glue: move workers from G.1X to G.2X,
p0.c1 -> avoid collect() on large DataFrames, and check for skewed
p0.c2 -> join keys before adding workers.
p1.c3 -> Missing watermark: the job falls back to a full load, which
p1.c4 -> takes about 30 minutes for 100 GB.

    5. Contextual chunks

    Before embedding, ask a model to write one sentence that situates the chunk in its document, and prepend it. Cost: one LLM call per chunk at index time (cheap when the whole document is in a cached prompt prefix). Benefit: chunks such as "Revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter" stop being ambiguous.

    contextual.py: the prompt and the plumbing (pass in any llm function)Python
    CONTEXT_PROMPT = """<document>
{document}
</document>
Here is a chunk from the document above:
<chunk>
{chunk}
</chunk>
Write one short sentence that situates this chunk within the overall document, to improve search retrieval.
Answer only with the sentence."""

def contextualise(document: str, chunks: list[str], llm) -> list[str]:
    out = []
    for c in chunks:
        context = llm(CONTEXT_PROMPT.format(document=document, chunk=c)).strip()
        out.append(f"{context}\n{c}")                 # embed AND keyword-index this combined text
    return out

fake_llm = lambda prompt: "From the Q3 2026 Marlo pipeline postmortem, root-cause section."
print(contextualise("<full postmortem>", ["Runs exceeded the timeout after the API added pagination."], fake_llm)[0])
    OutputOutput
    From the Q3 2026 Marlo pipeline postmortem, root-cause section.
Runs exceeded the timeout after the API added pagination.

    Choosing a size: measure it

    1. Build 30–50 questions with the chunk (or document section) that answers each.
    2. Index the corpus three times: e.g. 200, 400 and 800 tokens, same strategy.
    3. Measure recall@5 for each, and answer faithfulness on a sample.
    4. Pick the smallest size that keeps recall high; consider parent–child if small chunks retrieve well but answers lack context.
    SymptomLikely chunking causeTry
    Right document found, answer incompleteChunks too small; answer spans chunksLarger chunks, more overlap, parent–child
    Wrong chunks rank above right onesChunks too big; embedding averages several topicsSmaller chunks, structure-aware splits
    Questions using document names or sections missChunks lack contextHeading breadcrumb, contextual prefix
    Table questions failRows split from headersRow sentences with headers; table summary chunk
    Interview: How do you decide on a chunking strategy?

    "From the documents and the questions, then with measurements. If documents have structure, I split on headings and paragraphs first and prepend a breadcrumb of title and section path, because that context improves matching a lot. Size starts around 300 to 500 tokens with modest overlap. For long unstructured text like transcripts I'd consider semantic chunking. If small chunks retrieve well but answers lack context, I use parent–child: index the small chunks, send the parent section. If chunks are ambiguous out of context, I add a contextual sentence generated per chunk at index time. Then I compare variants on a labelled set with recall@5 and faithfulness and keep the cheapest one that performs."

    RAG · hands-on

    Local RAG stack: token chunks, LLM chunking, Chroma/Qdrant, cross-encoders

    Not every RAG system runs on managed AWS services. For prototypes, tests and on-prem work you'll use token-accurate chunking, open-source vector databases and local rerankers. This lesson covers the pieces and the trade-offs.

    1. Chunk by tokens, not characters

    Embedding models have token limits, and chunk sizes in papers and docs are given in tokens. Count with the right tokenizer: tiktoken for OpenAI-style models, the model's own tokenizer (Hugging Face) for open models, or the provider's count-tokens API.

    Token-based chunks with overlap (pip install tiktoken; the first call downloads the encoding)Python
    import tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")

def token_chunks(text: str, size: int = 300, overlap: int = 40) -> list[str]:
    ids = enc.encode(text)
    step = size - overlap
    return [enc.decode(ids[i:i + size]) for i in range(0, max(len(ids) - overlap, 1), step)]

# or with LangChain: RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter.from_tiktoken_encoder(chunk_size=300, chunk_overlap=40)

    2. LLM ("agentic") chunking

    Ask a model to split a document into self-contained sections and give each a title. It produces the most meaningful boundaries for messy text (meeting notes, long emails, transcripts), at the cost of one model call per document and less predictability. Validate the output: every character of the source should land in exactly one chunk.

    llm_chunking.py: model proposes boundaries, code validates coverage (runs offline with a fake model)Python
    import json

PROMPT = """Split the text into self-contained sections about one topic each.
Return JSON: [{{"title": "...", "start": <first sentence number>, "end": <last sentence number>}}].
Sentences:
{numbered}"""

def llm_chunk(sentences: list[str], llm) -> list[dict]:
    numbered = "\n".join(f"{i}: {s}" for i, s in enumerate(sentences))
    spans = json.loads(llm(PROMPT.format(numbered=numbered)))
    covered = sorted(i for s in spans for i in range(s["start"], s["end"] + 1))
    if covered != list(range(len(sentences))):          # gaps or overlaps: fall back to a safe splitter
        raise ValueError("model boundaries don't cover the text exactly")
    return [{"title": s["title"], "text": " ".join(sentences[s["start"]: s["end"] + 1])} for s in spans]

sents = ["Standup notes 17 Nov.", "The Quantum load ran out of memory again.", "We will move it to G.2X.",
         "Separately, Italy's API token expires Friday.", "Ravi will rotate the secret."]
fake = lambda p: '[{"title": "Quantum OOM", "start": 0, "end": 2}, {"title": "Italy token", "start": 3, "end": 4}]'
for c in llm_chunk(sents, fake):
    print(c["title"], "|", c["text"])
    OutputOutput
    Quantum OOM | Standup notes 17 Nov. The Quantum load ran out of memory again. We will move it to G.2X.
