      Workflows

      An event-driven RAG workflow with a relevance checkPython
      from llama_index.core.workflow import Workflow, step, Event, StartEvent, StopEvent

class Retrieved(Event):
    question: str
    nodes: list

class CheckedRAG(Workflow):
    @step
    async def retrieve(self, ev: StartEvent) -> Retrieved:
        nodes = index.as_retriever(similarity_top_k=8).retrieve(ev.question)
        return Retrieved(question=ev.question, nodes=nodes)

    @step
    async def answer(self, ev: Retrieved) -> StopEvent:
        good = [n for n in ev.nodes if n.score and n.score > 0.35]
        if not good:
            return StopEvent(result="No relevant runbook found.")
        context = "\n\n".join(n.get_content() for n in good[:4])
        r = await Settings.llm.acomplete(f"Answer from context only.\n{context}\n\nQ: {ev.question}")
        return StopEvent(result=str(r))

print(asyncio.run(CheckedRAG(timeout=60).run(question="How are backdated files handled?")))
      Interview: LlamaIndex vs LangChain for RAG?

      "Both can do it. LlamaIndex is more opinionated about the data side: ingestion pipelines, node parsing, many index and retriever types, query engines with built-in rerankers, sub-question decomposition and routers, and LlamaParse for messy documents. LangChain gives a broad integration library and its strength now is agents and middleware on LangGraph. A common production combo is LlamaIndex for indexing and retrieval, exposed as a tool to a LangGraph or Strands agent."

      Frameworks · llama-index 0.14 · hands-on

      LlamaIndex in depth: ingestion, indexes, query engines, workflows

      LlamaIndex's strength is the data side of RAG: a caching, de-duplicating ingestion pipeline, many node parsers, retrievers with filters and post-processors, query engines that combine retrieval and synthesis, and event-driven Workflows. Everything below runs offline with LlamaIndex's mock model and embeddings.

      The vocabulary

      TermMeaningLangChain equivalent
      DocumentA source item with text and metadataDocument
      NodeA chunk, with links to its document and neighboursSplit Document
      Node parser / transformationTurns documents into nodes (splitters, Markdown, semantic, hierarchical) or enriches them (extractors)Text splitter
      IngestionPipelineOrdered transformations with caching and a docstore for de-duplicationYour own indexing code
      IndexA structure over nodes, usually VectorStoreIndexVector store
      RetrieverReturns scored nodes for a queryRetriever
      Node postprocessorFilters, reranks or expands retrieved nodesCustom step / reranker
      Query engineRetriever + postprocessors + response synthesizerRAG chain
      WorkflowEvent-driven steps for custom flows and agentsLangGraph
      li_ingest.py: pipeline with de-duplication, metadata filters, a workflow (runs offline)Python
      import asyncio, warnings
from llama_index.core import Settings, VectorStoreIndex, Document
from llama_index.core.llms import MockLLM
from llama_index.core.embeddings import MockEmbedding
from llama_index.core.node_parser import MarkdownNodeParser, SentenceSplitter
from llama_index.core.ingestion import IngestionPipeline, DocstoreStrategy
from llama_index.core.storage.docstore import SimpleDocumentStore
from llama_index.core.vector_stores import MetadataFilters, MetadataFilter, FilterOperator
from llama_index.core.workflow import Workflow, step, Event, StartEvent, StopEvent
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

Settings.llm = MockLLM(max_tokens=20)                 # real: BedrockConverse(model="<id>", region_name="us-east-1")
Settings.embed_model = MockEmbedding(embed_dim=16)    # real: BedrockEmbedding(model_name="amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0")

docs = [Document(text="# OOM\nMove Glue workers to G.2X.", doc_id="oom.md", metadata={"team": "dp", "region": "JP"}),
        Document(text="# Watermark\nA missing watermark triggers a full load.", doc_id="wm.md", metadata={"team": "dp", "region": "IT"})]

pipeline = IngestionPipeline(
    transformations=[MarkdownNodeParser(), SentenceSplitter(chunk_size=256, chunk_overlap=20), Settings.embed_model],
    docstore=SimpleDocumentStore(), docstore_strategy=DocstoreStrategy.DUPLICATES_ONLY)   # UPSERTS needs vector_store=
nodes = pipeline.run(documents=docs)
print("first run nodes:", len(nodes), "| second run (unchanged docs):", len(pipeline.run(documents=docs)))
docs[0] = Document(text="# OOM\nMove Glue workers to G.2X and avoid collect().", doc_id="oom.md", metadata={"team": "dp", "region": "JP"})
print("after editing one doc:", len(pipeline.run(documents=docs)), "node re-processed")

index = VectorStoreIndex(nodes)
jp_only = MetadataFilters(filters=[MetadataFilter(key="region", value="JP", operator=FilterOperator.EQ)])
for hit in index.as_retriever(similarity_top_k=3, filters=jp_only).retrieve("memory errors"):
    print(hit.node.metadata["region"], "|", hit.node.get_content().replace("\n", " "))

class Retrieved(Event):
    question: str
    nodes: list

class CheckedRAG(Workflow):
    @step
    async def retrieve(self, ev: StartEvent) -> Retrieved:
        return Retrieved(question=ev.question, nodes=index.as_retriever(similarity_top_k=2).retrieve(ev.question))
    @step
    async def answer(self, ev: Retrieved) -> StopEvent:
        if not ev.nodes:
            return StopEvent(result="I don't know.")
        return StopEvent(result=f"would answer '{ev.question}' from {len(ev.nodes)} nodes")

async def main():
    return await CheckedRAG(timeout=30).run(question="glue oom?")
print(asyncio.run(main()))
      OutputOutput
      first run nodes: 2 | second run (unchanged docs): 0
after editing one doc: 1 node re-processed
JP | # OOM Move Glue workers to G.2X.
would answer 'glue oom?' from 2 nodes

      Query engines: retrieval + synthesis in one object

      Query engine options (real models)Python
      from llama_index.core.postprocessor import SimilarityPostprocessor
from llama_index.core.query_engine import RouterQueryEngine, SubQuestionQueryEngine
from llama_index.core.tools import QueryEngineTool

runbooks_qe = index.as_query_engine(
    similarity_top_k=8,
    node_postprocessors=[SimilarityPostprocessor(similarity_cutoff=0.35)],    # drop weak matches; add a reranker here too
    response_mode="compact")                         # refine | compact | tree_summarize | simple_summarize | no_text
resp = runbooks_qe.query("How do I fix a Glue heap space error?")
print(resp.response, [n.node.metadata for n in resp.source_nodes])          # answer + the nodes it used

tools = [QueryEngineTool.from_defaults(runbooks_qe, name="runbooks", description="How-to and fixes for pipelines"),
         QueryEngineTool.from_defaults(postmortems_qe, name="postmortems", description="Past incidents and root causes")]
router = RouterQueryEngine.from_defaults(query_engine_tools=tools)          # an LLM picks the engine per question
compare = SubQuestionQueryEngine.from_defaults(query_engine_tools=tools)    # splits into sub-questions per engine
      response_modeHow it builds the answerUse
      compact (default)Packs as many chunks as fit per call, refines across callsGeneral use
      refineOne call per chunk, improving the answer each timeDetailed answers; slow
      tree_summarizeSummarises chunks bottom-upSummaries over many chunks
      no_textRetrieval onlyWhen you generate elsewhere

      Agents in LlamaIndex

      FunctionAgent and multi-agent AgentWorkflow on BedrockPython
      from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent, AgentWorkflow
from llama_index.llms.bedrock_converse import BedrockConverse      # pip install llama-index-llms-bedrock-converse

llm = BedrockConverse(model="<model id>", region_name="us-east-1", temperature=0)
docs_agent = FunctionAgent(name="docs", description="Answers how-to questions from runbooks",
                           tools=[tools[0]], llm=llm, system_prompt="Answer from runbooks with citations.",
                           can_handoff_to=["sql"])
sql_agent = FunctionAgent(name="sql", description="Answers numeric questions with Athena SQL",
                          tools=[run_athena_sql], llm=llm, system_prompt="Write and run Athena SQL.")

# result = await team.run(user_msg="How many OOM failures this week, and what's the fix?")
      Interview: When would you choose LlamaIndex over LangChain or LangGraph?

      "When the hard part is the data: many source types, careful parsing and chunking, ingestion with caching and de-duplication, several indexes, and retrieval features such as post-processors, routers and sub-question engines out of the box. Its query engine bundles retrieval and synthesis, and Workflows give event-driven orchestration with agents and handoffs. I'd lean to LangGraph when the hard part is control flow, durable state and approvals. They combine fine: a LlamaIndex query engine can be a tool inside a LangGraph or Strands agent."

      Same agent in every framework

      One task, five implementations: an agent with a row_count(table, day) tool answering "Did qm_trusted lose rows on Nov 2?". Switch tabs and notice what stays the same: model, tool, prompt, loop.

      What to notice

      Every version turns a Python function's signature and docstring into the same JSON tool spec you wrote by hand, and every version runs the same Converse tool loop underneath. The differences are where state lives, how you add control (graph edges, hooks, middleware, Flows, Workflows) and what's built in for deployment and tracing.

      Frameworks · compare

      Other frameworks: OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK and the rest

      LangGraph, Strands, CrewAI and LlamaIndex cover most AWS work, but interviewers and job descriptions mention others. Know what each is, its core abstractions, and when you'd consider it. Versions below were checked on 17 November 2026.

      The OpenAI Agents SDK shape (for recognition in interviews)Python
      from agents import Agent, Runner, function_tool, InputGuardrail, GuardrailFunctionOutput

@function_tool
def row_count(table: str) -> int:
    """Rows loaded into a table today."""
    return 0

billing = Agent(name="billing", instructions="Handle invoice questions.")
ops = Agent(name="ops", instructions="Investigate data pipeline problems.", tools=[row_count])
triage = Agent(name="triage", instructions="Route the user to the right specialist.", handoffs=[billing, ops])
# result = await Runner.run(triage, "Why is marlo_orders empty?"); print(result.final_output)
      The Google ADK shapePython
      from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent, SequentialAgent

investigator = LlmAgent(name="investigator", model="<model>", instruction="Find why the job failed.", tools=[row_count])
writer = LlmAgent(name="writer", model="<model>", instruction="Write a two-line incident note from the findings.")
pipeline = SequentialAgent(name="incident_pipeline", sub_agents=[investigator, writer])
      The concepts transfer

      Every framework has the same parts: a model wrapper, tools from functions, an agent loop, some form of multi-agent composition (handoffs, sub-agents, graphs), guardrails or hooks, sessions/memory and tracing. If you can explain those in one framework and map them in another, you can pick up any of them in a day. On AWS, any of these can run on AgentCore Runtime and use Bedrock models (directly or via LiteLLM).

      Interview: A job description asks for the OpenAI Agents SDK, but you've used LangGraph and Strands. How do you answer?

      "I'd map concepts: in the Agents SDK an Agent has instructions, tools and handoffs, the Runner runs the loop, function_tool turns functions into tools, handoffs move control to another agent, and guardrails validate inputs and outputs. In LangGraph those are the agent node, ToolNode, Command-based handoffs and middleware or nodes for checks; in Strands they're Agent, @tool, swarm handoffs and hooks. The production concerns are the same: state, tracing, budgets, approvals and evals. I'd be productive quickly, and I'd keep tools behind MCP so they're portable across frameworks."

      Production on AWS

      Bedrock AgentCore map

      AgentCore is a set of managed services for running agents in production, built with any framework (Strands, LangGraph, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Agents SDK) and any model. Use the pieces you need; they work independently. Your AgentCore Runtime Handbook covers the hands-on deployment; this lesson is the interview map.

      ComponentWhat it doesStatus
      RuntimeHosts agent or tool code serverlessly with per-session microVM isolation, long sessions (up to 8 hours), streaming, and HTTP/MCP/A2A protocols. Bring a container or a Python entrypoint.GA Oct 2025
      HarnessManaged agent loop from a declarative definition (model, tools, skills, instructions); filesystem, shell, memory, browser per session; switch models mid-session; export to Strands code. No extra charge beyond the AgentCore pieces used.GA Jun 2026
      GatewayTurns Lambda functions, OpenAPI/Smithy APIs and MCP servers into one MCP endpoint with auth and semantic tool searchGA
      PolicyRules (written in natural language or Cedar) checked by Gateway on every tool call, outside the agent code; can also apply Bedrock Guardrails (Jun 2026)GA Mar 2026
      MemoryShort-term events plus long-term records extracted by strategies (semantic facts, summaries, user preferences, episodic)GA
      IdentityInbound auth (Cognito, Okta, Entra ID) and outbound OAuth/API-key vault so agents act on behalf of usersGA
      Code Interpreter, BrowserSandboxed code execution and managed headless browsersGA
      ObservabilityOpenTelemetry traces, metrics and logs into CloudWatch GenAI observabilityGA
      Evaluations13 built-in evaluators (quality, safety, task completion, tool use) plus custom LLM or Lambda code judges; online (sampled live traces) and on-demand (CI)GA Mar 2026
      Agent RegistryCatalogue and approval workflow for agents and toolsGA Aug 2026
      The AgentCore CLI flow (details in your AgentCore Runtime Handbook)Terminal
      agentcore create --name OpsAgent        # scaffold a project (framework template or harness)
agentcore dev                           # run locally
agentcore deploy                        # package, push, create the Runtime endpoint
agentcore invoke --runtime OpsAgent --payload '{"prompt": "Which Glue jobs failed today?"}'
agentcore logs; agentcore traces        # debug
agentcore eval                          # run evaluations
agentcore export                        # harness → Strands code when you need custom orchestration
      Interview: AgentCore vs Bedrock Agents (classic)?

      "Bedrock Agents is the earlier fully managed, console-configured agent with action groups and knowledge bases: quick, but limited control over the loop. AgentCore is infrastructure for any framework and model: you bring your own agent code (or use the declarative harness) and get isolated runtime sessions, a tool gateway with policies, memory, identity, observability and evaluations. For new agentic systems I'd use AgentCore; Bedrock Agents still fits simple managed use cases."

      Interview: Why not just run the agent on Lambda or ECS?

      "You can, and for simple agents that's fine. But agents have long, stateful, bursty sessions: Lambda's 15-minute limit and shared execution environments are awkward, and on ECS you build session isolation, scaling to zero, auth, token vaults and tracing yourself. Runtime gives per-session microVM isolation, up to 8-hour sessions, and consumption pricing that doesn't bill while waiting on I/O for CPU. Gateway, Identity, Memory and Policy cover the pieces every team otherwise rebuilds."

      Production on AWS · hands-on

      AgentCore hands-on: Runtime, Memory, Gateway, Identity, tools

      The AgentCore map told you what each service is. This lesson shows the code and commands you'll write for each, with the SDK (bedrock-agentcore) and the AgentCore CLI 1.0. Your separate AgentCore Runtime Handbook has the full deployment walk-through; this is the interview-ready tour.

      1. Runtime: wrap any agent as an entrypoint

      app.py: one entrypoint, streaming optional, session id from the runtimePython
      from bedrock_agentcore.runtime import BedrockAgentCoreApp
from strands import Agent                                # or a LangGraph graph, CrewAI crew, plain boto3 loop

app = BedrockAgentCoreApp()
agent = Agent(model="<model id>", system_prompt="You are the data platform assistant.")

@app.entrypoint
def invoke(payload: dict, context) -> dict:
    # context.session_id identifies the runtime session (one microVM per session)
    result = agent(payload["prompt"])
    return {"answer": str(result)}

# streaming: make the entrypoint an async generator and `yield` chunks; the runtime streams them (SSE)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()                                            # local server on port 8080: POST /invocations, GET /ping
      AgentCore CLI 1.0: create, run locally, deploy, invoke, observeTerminal
      npm install -g @aws/agentcore          # the CLI ships as an npm package
agentcore create                       # scaffold a project (framework, model, protocol) with a CDK app
agentcore dev                          # run locally with hot reload
agentcore deploy                       # build and deploy to AgentCore Runtime
agentcore invoke '{"prompt": "Did qm_trusted_load fail?"}'
agentcore logs                         # runtime logs
agentcore traces                       # OpenTelemetry traces (Transaction Search on by default)
agentcore eval                         # run evaluations against the deployed agent
      Runtime facts worth knowing

      Each session runs in its own microVM, sessions can last up to 8 hours, protocols include HTTP, MCP and A2A. Platform version V2 starts from a snapshot for consistent cold starts, supports container images up to 10 GB, committed vCPU/memory baselines with burst, FUSE mounts, a build warm-up hook and an OverheadLatency metric.

      2. Memory: short-term events, long-term strategies

      memory.py: create a memory with strategies, write turns, retrieve long-term factsPython
      from bedrock_agentcore.memory import MemoryClient

mc = MemoryClient(region_name="us-east-1")
memory = mc.create_memory_and_wait(
    name="oncall_assistant_memory",
    strategies=[
        {"semanticMemoryStrategy": {"name": "facts", "namespaces": ["/users/{actorId}/facts"]}},
        {"userPreferenceMemoryStrategy": {"name": "prefs", "namespaces": ["/users/{actorId}/preferences"]}},
        {"summaryMemoryStrategy": {"name": "summaries", "namespaces": ["/summaries/{actorId}/{sessionId}"]}},
    ],
    event_expiry_days=30)                                         # short-term events expire
mid = memory["id"]

# short-term: append conversation turns as events
mc.create_event(memory_id=mid, actor_id="u42", session_id="s-17",
                messages=[("Our Quantum job uses G.2X workers now", "USER"), ("Noted.", "ASSISTANT")])
recent = mc.get_last_k_turns(memory_id=mid, actor_id="u42", session_id="s-17", k=5)

# long-term: strategies extract facts asynchronously; retrieve by meaning
facts = mc.retrieve_memories(memory_id=mid, namespace="/users/u42/facts", query="worker type for Quantum", top_k=3)

      3. Gateway: existing APIs become MCP tools

      Gateway is configured, not coded: create a gateway (inbound auth with Cognito, Okta, Entra ID or IAM), add targets (Lambda functions, OpenAPI or Smithy specs, Step Functions state machines, existing MCP servers, built-in connectors such as web search), and point any MCP client at its URL. Policies (Cedar or natural language) are checked on every tool call, and semantic tool search helps agents find the right tool among hundreds.

      Gateway with the CLI (resource commands need no project)Terminal
      agentcore gateway --help               # create gateways, add Lambda / OpenAPI / MCP / Step Functions targets
# then, from any framework, connect an MCP client to the gateway URL with a token from your identity provider

      Interview: Walk me through deploying an agent on AgentCore.

      "I wrap the agent, in any framework, in a BedrockAgentCoreApp entrypoint that takes the payload and the runtime context, using the session ID as the conversation key. Locally I run it with agentcore dev, then agentcore deploy builds and deploys it to Runtime, which gives each session its own microVM, IAM-scoped execution, and HTTP, MCP or A2A protocols. Tools come through Gateway, which turns my Lambdas, OpenAPI services and Step Functions workflows into MCP tools with inbound auth and Policy checks. Memory stores turns as events and extracts long-term facts and preferences with strategies, namespaced per user. Identity handles user sign-in and OAuth tokens for downstream APIs. Observability sends OpenTelemetry traces to CloudWatch, and Evaluations runs on-demand and online scoring. I'd check limits like session duration and image size, and use the V2 platform for faster, consistent cold starts."

      Production on AWS · system design

      Reference architecture: a data-platform agent

      A design you can draw in any system-design round: an assistant for data engineers and analysts that answers questions from runbooks and tickets, finds tables, runs safe SQL, checks job health, and opens tickets, with approvals and evals.

      Walk through a request

      1. User asks in Slack: "Why did Marlo IT enriched miss its SLA yesterday?" API Gateway authenticates via the IdP; the agent receives user ID and groups.
      2. A small model classifies intent (incident analysis) and loads relevant memory (user's team, preferred SQL dialect).
      3. The main model plans: check job runs → read logs → compare volumes → search past tickets.
      4. Tool calls go through Gateway; Policy allows run_sql only on the read-only workgroup and only on tables the user's groups can see (Lake Formation enforces it again).
      5. Results are trimmed (row caps, log excerpts) before going back to the model.
      6. The agent proposes "rerun with G.2X workers"; because that's a write, it pauses for approval in Slack.
      7. Every step is traced; tokens and cost are attributed to the user and team; a sample of traces is scored online.

      Non-functional decisions to say out loud

      Latency
      Stream tokens; route simple questions to a small model; cache prompt prefixes; parallel tool calls.
      Cost
      Budget per request (turns, tokens); batch for offline enrichment; measure cost per resolved question.
      Reliability
      Retries with backoff, model fallback, idempotent tools, checkpointed state, timeouts on every tool.
      Security
      On-behalf-of identity, least-privilege tools, Policy, Guardrails, no raw egress, full audit trail.
      Quality
      Golden set of 150 real questions; retrieval and trajectory metrics; release only if scores don't drop.
      IaC and CI/CD
      Terraform for Gateway, Runtime, Memory, KBs; prompts and tool specs versioned in Git; eval job gates deploys.

      Production on AWS

      Observability and LLMOps

      You can't debug or improve an agent you can't see. Trace every model call and tool call with inputs, outputs, tokens, latency, cost and errors, grouped into one trace per request.

      What to capture per span

      SpanAttributes
      Request (root)user/tenant, session/thread id, app version, prompt version, total cost, final status, user feedback
      Model callmodel id, input/output/cached/thinking tokens, latency, time to first token, stop reason, temperature
      Tool calltool name, arguments (redacted), result size, duration, error, retries, approval decision
      Retrievalquery, index, top-k ids and scores, filters applied

      The industry standard is OpenTelemetry with the GenAI semantic conventions (gen_ai.* attributes). Strands emits OTel natively; LangChain/LangGraph trace to LangSmith and can export OTel; AgentCore Observability collects OTel into CloudWatch GenAI observability. Langfuse and Arize Phoenix are popular open-source backends.

      Send Strands or AgentCore traces to CloudWatch (ADOT auto-instrumentation)Terminal
      pip install aws-opentelemetry-distro
export OTEL_PYTHON_DISTRO=aws_distro OTEL_PYTHON_CONFIGURATOR=aws_configurator
export AGENT_OBSERVABILITY_ENABLED=true
opentelemetry-instrument python app.py
      LangChain/LangGraph → LangSmithTerminal
      export LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
export LANGSMITH_API_KEY=...
export LANGSMITH_PROJECT=ops-agent-prod

      The LLMOps loop

      Fine-tuning and efficiency (enough for interviews)

      LoRA / QLoRA
      Train small adapters; QLoRA on a 4-bit base model. Cheap, swappable per task.
      Bedrock customisation
      Fine-tuning, continued pre-training, distillation (big teacher → small student), reinforcement fine-tuning for supported models; custom model import for your own weights.
      When it pays off
      High-volume narrow tasks where a fine-tuned small model matches a big one at a fraction of cost and latency; strict formats; domain language.
      Serving open models
      vLLM or TGI on SageMaker/EKS: continuous batching, paged KV cache, quantisation (AWQ, GPTQ, FP8), speculative decoding.

      Production on AWS · hands-on

      Tracing lab: OpenTelemetry spans for an agent

      Frameworks emit traces for you, but you should know what a good trace contains and be able to add spans to your own code. This lab instruments a small agent loop with OpenTelemetry using the GenAI semantic-convention attribute names, captures the spans in memory, and prints the trace tree.

      otel_agent.py: one trace per request, spans for model and tool calls (runs offline)Python
      import json, time
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export.in_memory_span_exporter import InMemorySpanExporter

exporter = InMemorySpanExporter()                   # production: OTLP exporter -> CloudWatch / Langfuse / LangSmith
provider = TracerProvider(); provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(exporter))
tracer = provider.get_tracer("oncall-agent")

def fake_model(messages):                           # stand-in for a Bedrock call
    if not any(m["role"] == "tool" for m in messages):
        return {"tool_call": {"name": "row_count", "args": {"table": "marlo_orders"}}, "usage": (812, 24)}
    return {"text": "marlo_orders loaded 0 rows.", "usage": (901, 12)}

def call_model(messages):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("chat") as span:
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "chat")
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", "<model id>")
        out = fake_model(messages)
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", out["usage"][0])
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", out["usage"][1])
        return out

def call_tool(name, args):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span(f"execute_tool {name}") as span:
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "execute_tool")
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.tool.name", name)
        span.set_attribute("tool.args", json.dumps(args))          # redact sensitive arguments in real systems
        return 0

def handle(question: str, user: str, prompt_version: str = "v12"):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("invoke_agent oncall") as root:
        root.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "invoke_agent")
        root.set_attribute("app.user_id", user); root.set_attribute("app.prompt_version", prompt_version)
        messages = [{"role": "user", "content": question}]
        for _ in range(5):
            out = call_model(messages)
            if "tool_call" not in out:
                root.set_attribute("app.status", "answered")
                return out["text"]
            result = call_tool(out["tool_call"]["name"], out["tool_call"]["args"])
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": str(result)})

print(handle("Why is marlo_orders empty?", user="u42"))
spans = sorted(exporter.get_finished_spans(), key=lambda s: s.start_time)
ids = {s.context.span_id: s for s in spans}
for s in spans:
    depth = 0; p = s.parent
    while p is not None:
        depth += 1; p = ids[p.span_id].parent if p.span_id in ids else None
    a = s.attributes
    detail = {k.split(".")[-1]: v for k, v in a.items() if k.startswith(("gen_ai.usage", "gen_ai.tool", "app."))}
    print("  " * depth + s.name, detail)
total_in = sum(s.attributes.get("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", 0) for s in spans)
print("input tokens for this request:", total_in)
      OutputOutput
      marlo_orders loaded 0 rows.
invoke_agent oncall {'user_id': 'u42', 'prompt_version': 'v12', 'status': 'answered'}
  chat {'input_tokens': 812, 'output_tokens': 24}
  execute_tool row_count {'name': 'row_count'}
  chat {'input_tokens': 901, 'output_tokens': 12}
input tokens for this request: 1713

      On AWS without writing spans by hand

      Strands and AgentCore emit OpenTelemetry natively; LangChain/LangGraph can be instrumented with OpenTelemetry instrumentations or traced to LangSmith. Install the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (aws-opentelemetry-distro) and enable CloudWatch Transaction Search to see traces in CloudWatch GenAI observability. Add your own attributes (tenant, prompt version, eval scores) to the framework's spans.

      Interview: What would you put in a trace for an LLM agent?

      "One root span per user request with tenant, user, session, app and prompt versions and the final status. Under it, a span per model call with model ID, input, output and cached tokens, latency, time to first token and stop reason, and a span per tool call with tool name, redacted arguments, result size, duration and errors; retrieval spans carry the query, index, filters and returned chunk IDs with scores. I use the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions so any backend understands it, export via OTLP to CloudWatch or Langfuse, and control access because prompts and outputs are sensitive. Then dashboards for cost per request, latency by span type and loop counts, and online evaluators attached to sampled traces."

      Production · hands-on

      Cost and latency engineering

      A demo that costs 40 cents and takes 25 seconds per answer is not a product. Cost and latency come from the same few sources, and there is a standard order in which to attack them. Interviewers ask this as "your bill doubled" or "p95 is 20 seconds, fix it".

      Where the time and money go

      SourceDrivesFirst fix
      Output tokensLatency (generated one by one) and cost (priciest tokens)Ask for shorter answers, set maxTokens, structured output instead of prose
      Input tokens re-sent every turnCost, some latencyPrompt caching, trim history, fewer and smaller chunks, compact tool results
      Number of LLM calls per requestBoth, multipliedFewer agent turns, parallel tool calls, workflows instead of free loops
      Model sizeBothRoute easy work to a small model; reserve the large model for hard steps
      Reasoning / thinking tokensBothLower the effort or budget for simple steps
      Tools and retrievalLatencyRun in parallel, add timeouts, cache results, tune the index
      Cold starts and throttling retriesTail latencyWarm capacity, cross-Region inference, backoff with jitter

      Lever 1: prompt caching

      If many requests start with the same long prefix (system prompt, tool definitions, a policy document), mark the end of that prefix with a cache point. The first call writes the cache; later calls within the cache lifetime read it at a fraction of the input price and skip re-processing it. The prefix must be byte-identical, so keep anything that changes (date, user name, question) after the cache point.

      Prompt caching with Converse: stable prefix first, cache point, then the variable partPython
      import os, boto3
brt = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1")
RUNBOOK = open("oncall_runbook.md").read()            # long and identical for every request

def ask(question: str) -> str:
    resp = brt.converse(
        modelId=os.environ["BEDROCK_MODEL_ID"],
        system=[{"text": "You are the on-call assistant. Answer from the runbook below.\n\n" + RUNBOOK},
                {"cachePoint": {"type": "default"}}],                 # everything above is cached
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": question}]}], # everything below changes per call
        inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 400, "temperature": 0},
    )
    u = resp["usage"]
    print(f'in={u["inputTokens"]} cache_write={u.get("cacheWriteInputTokens", 0)} '
          f'cache_read={u.get("cacheReadInputTokens", 0)} out={u["outputTokens"]}')
    return resp["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"]

ask("Glue job OOM: first step?")       # first call: cache_write > 0
ask("Who do I page for Marlo?")        # second call: cache_read > 0, lower cost and latency
      Caching rules that trip people up

      Caches expire after a short idle time (minutes), models have a minimum cacheable prefix length, and cache writes cost a little more than normal input. Caching pays off when the same prefix is reused several times within the lifetime. Putting a timestamp or request ID at the top of the system prompt silently disables it. Check cacheReadInputTokens in your logs to prove it's working.

      Lever 2: route by difficulty

      A two-tier router: cheap model first, escalate only when neededPython
      SMALL, LARGE = "small-model", "large-model"       # in real code: two Bedrock model IDs from config

def pick_model(task: dict) -> str:
    """Rule-based routing is the usual starting point: transparent, free and easy to evaluate."""
    if task["kind"] in {"classify", "extract", "grade", "rewrite_query", "summarise_tool_output"}:
        return SMALL
    if task.get("tools_needed", 0) > 2 or task.get("input_tokens", 0) > 30_000:
        return LARGE
    if task["kind"] in {"plan", "final_answer", "sql_generation", "code"}:
        return LARGE
    return SMALL

for t in [{"kind": "grade"}, {"kind": "final_answer"}, {"kind": "qa", "tools_needed": 4}, {"kind": "qa"}]:
    print(t, "->", pick_model(t))
      OutputOutput
      {'kind': 'grade'} -> small-model
{'kind': 'final_answer'} -> large-model
{'kind': 'qa', 'tools_needed': 4} -> large-model
{'kind': 'qa'} -> small-model

      Managed option: Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing picks between models in a family per request. Whatever does the routing, evaluate each route on your own eval set: a router that saves 60% and drops accuracy five points may or may not be a good trade.

      Lever 3: cache answers

      A semantic cache: reuse an answer when a new question means the same thingPython
      import zlib
import numpy as np

class SemanticCache:
    def __init__(self, embed, threshold: float = 0.92):
        self.embed, self.threshold = embed, threshold
        self.vecs, self.items = [], []                # production: MemoryDB/Valkey vector search with TTL

    def get(self, question: str, scope: str):
        if not self.vecs:
            return None
        q = self.embed(question)
        sims = np.array(self.vecs) @ q
        i = int(sims.argmax())
        hit = self.items[i]
        if sims[i] >= self.threshold and hit["scope"] == scope:      # never share across tenants/permissions
            return hit["answer"]
        return None

    def put(self, question: str, scope: str, answer: str):
        self.vecs.append(self.embed(question)); self.items.append({"scope": scope, "answer": answer})

def toy_embed(text: str) -> np.ndarray:               # stand-in so this runs offline; use a real embedding model
    v = np.zeros(64)
    for w in text.lower().replace("?", "").split():
        v[zlib.crc32(w.encode()) % 64] += 1
    return v / (np.linalg.norm(v) or 1)

cache = SemanticCache(toy_embed, threshold=0.8)
cache.put("how do I fix a glue job out of memory error", "team-a", "Move to G.2X and avoid collect().")
print(cache.get("how do I fix glue job out of memory error", "team-a"))    # near-duplicate, same scope
print(cache.get("how do I fix glue job out of memory error", "team-b"))    # different scope
print(cache.get("when does the marlo pipeline run", "team-a"))             # different question
      OutputOutput
      Move to G.2X and avoid collect().

      Prompt cache (provider)Identical prefixLong system prompts, tool lists, documentsNone for correctness; only savings
      Exact response cacheHash of full requestRepeated identical calls, evals, retriesStale data if sources change
      Semantic cacheEmbedding similarityFAQ-style trafficFalse hits ("in Japan" vs "in Italy"); leaking across users. Scope the key, set a TTL, keep the threshold high
      Tool / retrieval cacheTool name + argsSlow lookups repeated within a runStale results; cache only read-only tools

      Lever 4: make it feel fast

      Streaming with ConverseStream: time to first token is what users noticePython
      import os, time, boto3
brt = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1")

t0 = time.time(); first = None
resp = brt.converse_stream(
    modelId=os.environ["BEDROCK_MODEL_ID"],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Explain Iceberg snapshot expiry in 5 bullet points."}]}],
    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 400})
for event in resp["stream"]:
    if "contentBlockDelta" in event:
        first = first or time.time() - t0
        print(event["contentBlockDelta"]["delta"].get("text", ""), end="", flush=True)
    elif "metadata" in event:
        usage = event["metadata"]["usage"]
print(f"\n\nTTFT {first:.2f}s  total {time.time() - t0:.2f}s  out tokens {usage['outputTokens']}")

      Measure three numbers separately: TTFT (time to first token), tokens per second, and total time. Streaming improves the first without changing the last. For agents, also stream progress events ("searching runbooks…", "running query…") so a 20-second task doesn't look frozen.

      Lever 5: don't do it in real time

      Classification, extraction, summarisation and embedding of large backlogs don't need an instant answer. Bedrock batch inference takes JSONL from S3 and returns results to S3 at a lower price than on-demand. For a data engineer this is the natural shape: an LLM step inside a Glue, Step Functions or Airflow pipeline.

      The order to apply them

      1. Measure: log tokens, calls and latency per request, tagged by feature. Use Bedrock cost breakdowns in Cost Explorer and application inference profiles for per-team attribution.
      2. Cut waste: shorter outputs, fewer chunks, trimmed tool results, capped history.
      3. Cache the stable prefix.
      4. Route simple steps to a small model.
      5. Parallelise independent tool calls and retrieval.
      6. Batch whatever can wait.
      7. Only then consider fine-tuning or distilling a small model, or provisioned capacity for steady high volume.

      After every change, rerun the eval set. Cost optimisation without a quality check is just making the product worse cheaply.

      Interview: p95 latency for your agent is 25 seconds. How do you bring it down?

      "I'd break the trace into spans first: model calls, tool calls, retrieval, and count turns. Usually it's too many sequential LLM turns and long outputs. So: reduce turns by giving the agent better task-level tools and letting it call tools in parallel; cap and shorten outputs; move grading, routing and summarising steps to a small fast model; cache the system prompt and tool definitions; add timeouts and caching to slow tools. For perceived latency I'd stream tokens and progress events so time to first token is under a couple of seconds. For tail latency I'd look at throttling retries and cold starts: cross-Region inference profiles, backoff with jitter, and on AgentCore Runtime V2 the snapshot starts and the OverheadLatency metric to separate platform time from my code. I'd confirm quality held on the eval set."

      Interview: How does prompt caching differ from a semantic cache?

      "Prompt caching is done by the model provider: it stores the processed form of an identical prompt prefix, so the next request with that same prefix is cheaper and faster, but the model still generates a fresh answer. It's safe for correctness. A semantic cache is something I build: it stores final answers keyed by the embedding of the question and returns a stored answer when a new question is similar enough, skipping the model completely. That saves more but can return a wrong answer on a near-miss or leak across users, so it needs a high similarity threshold, a TTL, and a cache key scoped by tenant and permissions."

      Production · hands-on

      Reliability: retries, fallbacks, quotas and idempotency

      LLM APIs fail more often than the databases you're used to: throttling, timeouts, overloaded models, malformed outputs. A production system assumes every call can fail and decides in advance what happens next.

      The errors you will see on Bedrock

      ErrorMeaningDo
      ThrottlingException (429)Over your requests-per-minute or tokens-per-minute quotaRetry with exponential backoff and jitter; smooth traffic; request a quota increase; use cross-Region inference
      ServiceUnavailableException, InternalServerExceptionTemporary service problemRetry; then fall back
      ModelTimeoutException, read timeoutGeneration took too longRaise client read timeout for long outputs; stream; reduce output; fall back
      ModelNotReadyExceptionModel warming upRetry
      ValidationExceptionYour request is wrong (bad message order, too many tokens, bad schema)Do not retry; fix the request. Often means context overflow: trim and retry once
      AccessDeniedExceptionIAM or model access not grantedDo not retry; fix permissions
      Stop reason max_tokensAnswer cut offNot an exception: check stopReason on every response
      Stop reason guardrail_intervened / content filteredBlocked by a guardrailReturn a safe message; log it; don't retry blindly

      A call wrapper with retry and model fallback

      resilient.pyPython
      import os, random, time, boto3
from botocore.config import Config
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError, ReadTimeoutError

brt = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1",
                   config=Config(read_timeout=120, connect_timeout=5, retries={"max_attempts": 1}))  # we do our own retries

RETRYABLE = {"ThrottlingException", "ServiceUnavailableException", "InternalServerException",
             "ModelTimeoutException", "ModelNotReadyException"}
CHAIN = [os.environ["BEDROCK_MODEL_ID"],                       # primary
         os.environ.get("BEDROCK_FALLBACK_MODEL_ID", "")]      # e.g. another model or a cross-Region profile

def converse_resilient(messages, system=None, max_attempts=4, **kw):
    last = None
    for model in [m for m in CHAIN if m]:
        for attempt in range(max_attempts):
            try:
                resp = brt.converse(modelId=model, messages=messages, system=system or [], **kw)
                if resp["stopReason"] == "max_tokens":
                    resp["truncated"] = True                    # surface it; caller decides
                resp["model_used"] = model
                return resp
            except ReadTimeoutError as e:
                last = e
            except ClientError as e:
                last = e
                if e.response["Error"]["Code"] not in RETRYABLE:
                    raise                                       # validation / access errors: fail fast
            time.sleep(min(20, 2 ** attempt) * random.uniform(0.5, 1.0))   # exponential backoff + jitter
        # retries exhausted on this model: fall through to the next one in the chain
    raise RuntimeError(f"all models failed: {last}")
      Backoff with jitter
      Wait 1, 2, 4, 8… seconds, multiplied by a random factor. Without jitter, all your workers retry at the same instant and get throttled again.
      Fallback chain
      A second model or Region to try when the first is unavailable. The fallback may behave differently, so it must pass the same eval set. AgentCore Gateway can now do this at the platform level with ordered targets and a circuit breaker.
      Circuit breaker
      After N failures, stop calling the failing target for a cool-down period instead of making every request wait for a timeout.
      Cross-Region inference
      An inference profile routes requests to capacity in several Regions. It raises effective throughput and resilience; check data-residency rules before using a geography-wide or global profile.
      Timeouts everywhere
      On the model call, each tool, the whole agent run, and the user request. A missing timeout is how one stuck tool hangs a whole system.
      Graceful degradation
      If the reranker is down, answer from un-reranked results. If the LLM is down, return search results. Decide these in advance.

      Idempotency: the rule for anything that writes

      Agents retry, harnesses replay nodes after a crash, and users double-click. Any tool that changes state must be safe to call twice.

      An idempotent write tool using a DynamoDB conditional putPython
      import hashlib, json, boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

ddb = boto3.client("dynamodb"); glue = boto3.client("glue")

def rerun_glue_job(job_name: str, reason: str, run_key: str) -> dict:
    """Start a Glue job at most once per run_key. run_key comes from the harness (thread id + step), not the model."""
    key = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps([job_name, run_key]).encode()).hexdigest()
    try:
        ddb.put_item(TableName="agent_actions",
                     Item={"pk": {"S": key}, "job": {"S": job_name}, "reason": {"S": reason}, "state": {"S": "STARTING"}},
                     ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(pk)")         # first writer wins
    except ClientError as e:
        if e.response["Error"]["Code"] == "ConditionalCheckFailedException":
            prev = ddb.get_item(TableName="agent_actions", Key={"pk": {"S": key}})["Item"]
            return {"status": "already_done", "job_run_id": prev.get("job_run_id", {}).get("S"), "note": "Not started again."}
        raise
    run_id = glue.start_job_run(JobName=job_name, Arguments={"--triggered_by": "agent"})["JobRunId"]
    ddb.update_item(TableName="agent_actions", Key={"pk": {"S": key}},
                    UpdateExpression="SET job_run_id = :r, #s = :s", ExpressionAttributeNames={"#s": "state"},
                    ExpressionAttributeValues={":r": {"S": run_id}, ":s": {"S": "STARTED"}})
    return {"status": "started", "job_run_id": run_id}

      This is the same conditional-write pattern you'd use for exactly-once processing in a pipeline. Say that in an interview: it shows your data-engineering habits carry over.

      Quotas and throughput planning

      • Bedrock on-demand quotas are per model, per Region: requests per minute and tokens per minute. Agents burn tokens per minute fast because each turn re-sends the context.
      • Estimate: peak requests/min × average total tokens per request × average turns. Compare with your quota before launch, not after.
      • Options when you're short: quota increase, cross-Region inference profile, queue and smooth with SQS, smaller model for sub-steps, batch for offline work, provisioned or reserved capacity for steady high load.
      • Protect yourself from your own users: per-user and per-tenant rate limits and token budgets at the API layer.
      Interview: How do you make an LLM-based service reliable?

      "I assume every model and tool call can fail. Calls go through one wrapper with timeouts, retries with exponential backoff and jitter for throttling and transient errors, and no retry for validation or permission errors. There's a fallback chain to a second model or Region with a circuit breaker, and the fallback is tested on the same evals. I check stop reasons so truncated or guardrail-blocked outputs aren't treated as answers, and validate structured output with a repair retry. Write tools are idempotent with keys from the harness, and risky ones need approval. Agent runs have step, token and wall-clock budgets and are checkpointed so they resume after a crash. I plan capacity against tokens-per-minute quotas, queue bursts, and define degraded modes. Then alarms on error rate, latency, cost and eval scores."

      Interview: You get ThrottlingException in production at peak. What are your options?

      "Short term: retry with backoff and jitter, and smooth bursts with a queue so requests wait instead of failing. Check whether it's requests-per-minute or tokens-per-minute; with agents it's usually tokens, so trimming context and caching helps directly. Medium term: request a quota increase, switch to a cross-Region inference profile for more capacity, move sub-steps to a smaller model with its own quota, and push offline work to batch. For predictable high volume, buy provisioned or reserved capacity. I'd also add per-tenant limits so one heavy user can't exhaust the shared quota, and an alarm on throttle rate."

      Production on AWS · hands-on

      Serving an agent: FastAPI, streaming, async, queues and containers

      An agent becomes a product when it sits behind an API. This lesson builds that API: async endpoints, streaming tokens over server-sent events, parallel model calls with timeouts, background jobs for long tasks, and the container and AWS options to run it. The async demo and the FastAPI app both run offline.

      1. Async: don't let one slow call block everything

      parallel_timeout.py: ask three models at once, keep what returns in time (runs offline)Python
      import asyncio, time

async def call_model(name: str, delay: float) -> str:      # stand-in for an async Bedrock / HTTP call
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return f"{name} answered"

async def fan_out(timeout: float = 0.5) -> dict:
    tasks = {name: asyncio.create_task(call_model(name, d)) for name, d in [("small", 0.1), ("medium", 0.3), ("large", 2.0)]}
    done, pending = await asyncio.wait(tasks.values(), timeout=timeout)
    for t in pending:
        t.cancel()                                           # don't leave work running
    return {name: (t.result() if t in done else "timed out") for name, t in tasks.items()}

t = time.perf_counter()
print(asyncio.run(fan_out()), f"in {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s")
      OutputOutput
      {'small': 'small answered', 'medium': 'medium answered', 'large': 'timed out'} in 0.5s

      2. A streaming FastAPI endpoint

      api.py: JSON and SSE endpoints, tested in-process (runs offline; pip install fastapi httpx)Python
      import asyncio, json
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI(title="oncall-agent")

class Ask(BaseModel):
    question: str
    session_id: str

async def agent_stream(question: str):                     # real: async for ev in agent.astream(..., stream_mode=["messages","updates"])
    yield {"type": "status", "text": "searching runbooks"}
    for token in ["Move ", "the ", "job ", "to ", "G.2X ", "workers [1]."]:
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        yield {"type": "token", "text": token}
    yield {"type": "done", "sources": ["oom.md"]}

@app.post("/ask")
async def ask(req: Ask) -> dict:
    text = "".join([ev["text"] async for ev in agent_stream(req.question) if ev["type"] == "token"])
    return {"answer": text, "session_id": req.session_id}

@app.post("/ask/stream")
async def ask_stream(req: Ask):
    async def sse():
        async for ev in agent_stream(req.question):
            yield f"data: {json.dumps(ev)}\n\n"            # server-sent events format
    return StreamingResponse(sse(), media_type="text/event-stream")

@app.get("/health")
async def health():
    return {"ok": True}

client = TestClient(app)
print(client.post("/ask", json={"question": "glue oom?", "session_id": "s1"}).json())
with client.stream("POST", "/ask/stream", json={"question": "glue oom?", "session_id": "s1"}) as r:
    print([json.loads(line[6:])["type"] for line in r.iter_lines() if line.startswith("data: ")])
      OutputOutput
      {'answer': 'Move the job to G.2X workers [1].', 'session_id': 's1'}
['status', 'token', 'token', 'token', 'token', 'token', 'token', 'done']

      3. Long tasks: accept, queue, poll

      An investigation that takes five minutes should not hold an HTTP connection open. Return 202 Accepted with a job ID, put the work on a queue (SQS) or start a Step Functions execution, let workers run the agent with a checkpointer, and let the client poll or subscribe (WebSocket, push notification) for the result. Make the submit idempotent with a client-supplied request ID.

      4. Containerise and run on AWS

      Dockerfile for the APIText
      FROM public.ecr.aws/docker/library/python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
USER 1000
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["uvicorn", "api:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080", "--workers", "2"]
      OptionGood forNotes
      AgentCore RuntimeAgents specificallyPer-session isolation, long sessions, built-in streaming, Identity, Gateway, Observability
      ECS on Fargate behind an ALB or API GatewayYour own API with streaming, steady trafficConfigure ALB idle timeouts for SSE; autoscale on CPU or request count
      Lambda (with response streaming)Spiky, short requests15-minute limit; cold starts
      SQS / Step Functions workersLong or batch agent tasksDecouple submission from execution; retries and DLQs
      Production checklist for the API

      Authenticate every request (Cognito/JWT) and derive user context server-side; per-user rate limits and token budgets; timeouts on every downstream call; secrets from Secrets Manager; structured logs with trace IDs; health and readiness endpoints; graceful shutdown that lets streams finish; load-test with realistic streaming durations before launch.

      Interview: How would you serve an agent to a web UI?

      "Behind an async API, typically FastAPI. Short questions use an endpoint that streams server-sent events: status events for steps, token events for text and a final event with sources, which I get from the agent framework's stream modes. All downstream calls are async with timeouts, so one slow model or tool can't block the worker, and independent calls run in parallel. Long investigations are accepted with a job ID, queued to SQS or Step Functions and polled. Identity comes from the JWT on the server, with per-user rate limits and budgets. I containerise it and run it on ECS Fargate or wrap the agent for AgentCore Runtime, which gives session isolation and observability, with secrets in Secrets Manager and traces to CloudWatch."

      Production · process

      Shipping and operating: the LLMOps release loop

      Prompts, models, tools and retrieval settings are all "code" that changes behaviour. They need the same discipline as a pipeline release: versions, tests, staged rollout, monitoring and rollback. This is the process to describe when asked "how do you take an agent to production?"

      What to version

      ArtefactWhere it livesNote
      Prompts and tool descriptionsGit (or a prompt registry with version IDs)Reviewed like code; the version ID is logged with every request
      Model ID / inference profileConfig, pinned to an exact versionNever "latest". Model upgrades are releases that must pass evals
      Retrieval configConfig: embedding model, chunking, top-k, thresholdsIndex is versioned with the embedding model
      Guardrail configBedrock Guardrails versionUse numbered versions, not the working draft
      Eval dataset and gradersGit / S3 with a versionSo scores are comparable across runs
      Agent code and containerGit + ECR image tag; AgentCore Runtime version and endpointEndpoints let you point "prod" at a tested version and roll back by re-pointing

      Production readiness checklist

      Quality

      • Eval set of 50+ cases incl. edge and adversarial
      • CI gate with thresholds
      • Pass rate measured over several trials
      • Human-reviewed sample each week

      Safety and security

      • Least-privilege IAM role per agent
      • Guardrails on input and output; PII handling
      • Untrusted content treated as data
      • Approval for destructive or external actions
      • Access control in retrieval and tools, tested
      • Audit log of actions with user identity

      Reliability

      • Timeouts, retries, fallback, circuit breaker
      • Step, token and time budgets per run
      • Idempotent write tools
      • Checkpointed long runs
      • Load tested against quotas

      Operations

      • Traces with prompt/model/version IDs
      • Dashboards: latency, error rate, tokens, cost per request
      • Alarms on the above and on online eval scores
      • Feedback capture (thumbs, edits, escalations)
      • Runbook and rollback tested
      • Cost budget and per-tenant limits

      Rollout techniques

      Shadow mode
      The new version runs on real traffic but its output is only logged and scored, never shown. Zero user risk; best first step for model upgrades.
      Canary
      Send a small share of traffic to the new version, compare metrics, widen gradually.
      A/B test
      Split traffic and compare a business metric (resolution rate, edits, escalations), not just eval scores.
      Feature flag / kill switch
      Turn off a tool or the whole agent without a deploy.
      Rollback
      Re-point the endpoint or flag to the previous prompt, model and index versions together, since they were tested as a set.

      What to watch after launch

      SignalWhy
      Online eval scores on sampled traffic (faithfulness, helpfulness, goal success)Quality drift that latency and error dashboards can't see
      Refusal / "I don't know" rateRising means corpus gaps or over-strict guardrails
      Steps and tokens per run, tool error rateEarly sign of loops or a broken tool
      User feedback, edit rate, escalation to humanThe real outcome metric
      Cost per request and per tenantBudget control; spot abuse
      Index freshness lagStale answers
      Guardrail intervention rateAttacks or false positives
      On AWS

      AgentCore Observability sends OpenTelemetry traces to CloudWatch; AgentCore Evaluations can score sampled production sessions (online) and datasets (on-demand and batch), including the failure-analysis evaluator that groups failed sessions by root cause. Bedrock model invocation logging captures prompts and responses to S3 or CloudWatch Logs; treat those logs as sensitive data.

      Interview: A new model version is out and the team wants to switch. What's your process?

      "I treat it as a release. First I run the full offline eval set on the new model with current prompts and compare to the baseline per metric and per slice, plus cost and latency. Prompts tuned for the old model often need adjusting, so I iterate there. Then shadow traffic: the new model processes real requests but only logs, and online evaluators score both. Then a canary at a few percent with alarms on quality, error rate, latency and cost, widening in steps. Model ID is pinned in config so rollback is one change, and I keep the old version available until the new one has been stable. I'd also check the fallback chain and structured-output behaviour, since those break quietly."

      Senior data engineer · start here

      Your six years already count: the DE-to-agentic map

      You are not starting from zero. Most of what makes an agent system work in production is data engineering under new names. This chapter is written for someone with about six years on AWS (Glue, PySpark, Iceberg, Athena, Step Functions, Lambda, Lake Formation) and shows where each habit you already have plugs in, and where the new thinking really is new.

      The translation table

      What you do todayThe same idea in GenAI / agentsWhat is actually new
      Incremental load with a watermark in DynamoDBIncremental re-indexing: embed only new or changed chunksThe "row" is a chunk; the key is a content hash, because documents have no reliable updated_at
      Full-load fallback when the watermark is missingFull rebuild of an index when the embedding model or chunking changesA rebuild goes into a new index and you switch an alias; vectors from two models can't be mixed
      Landing → raw → trusted → enriched → business layersSource docs → parsed text → chunks → embeddings → served indexKeep every layer; when retrieval is bad you debug layer by layer exactly as you do now
      Idempotent jobs, safe re-runsIdempotent tools: an agent retries, a harness replaysThe caller is a model that may retry with slightly different arguments, so the idempotency key comes from the harness
      Data-quality checks and a reconciliation reportEvals: a dataset, graders, thresholds, a reportOutputs are text, so some checks need an LLM judge that you calibrate against human labels
      Audit table of files processedTraces: every model call, tool call and retrieval with inputs and outputsYou also log token usage and prompt/model version IDs
      Step Functions orchestration with retries and catchWorkflows; an agent is a step inside one, or the workflow is a tool the agent callsControl flow can be chosen by the model at run time; you bound it with budgets
      Lake Formation row/column securityAccess control at retrieval and tool timeThe agent must act with the end user's identity, never a broad service role
      PHI/PII masking in the trusted layerMasking before text reaches a model, a log or a vector indexPrompts, traces, caches and memories are new places sensitive data can leak
      Partition pruning, broadcast joins, AQEContext engineering: send the model only what it needsThe scarce resource is tokens in the window, not shuffle memory
      Cost per job, DPU-hoursCost per request, tokens per runCost grows with turns × context size; caching and routing are the tuning knobs
      Glue Data Catalog with descriptionsThe context an agent reads to find tables and write SQLCatalog quality now directly decides answer quality
      Schema evolutionPrompt, tool-schema and output-schema versioningA changed tool description is a behaviour change and needs an eval run
      BackfillsRe-running an LLM stage when the prompt or model changesKey outputs by input hash + prompt version + model version so backfills are selective
      SLA and freshness monitoringIndex freshness lag, online eval scores, refusal rateQuality can drift with no error and no latency change

      What is new and needs real study

      1. Non-determinism. The same input can give different outputs. You test with pass rates over several trials, never a single assert on a string.
      2. The model reads everything as text. Tool names, descriptions, error messages and retrieved documents are all prompt. Writing them well is engineering work.
      3. Untrusted content can carry instructions. Prompt injection has no equivalent in classic pipelines. Design so a hijacked model can't do damage.
      4. Evaluation of meaning. "Is this answer right?" has no row count. You need labelled cases and calibrated judges.
      5. Context as the bottleneck. Most agent failures are the model seeing too much, too little or the wrong thing.

      Three role shapes and how you fit

      RoleYour edgeGap to close first
      Agentic AI Data Engineer / AI Data Platform EngineerStrongest fit: pipelines that feed agents and agents that run pipelinesRAG internals, evals, MCP tool layer
      Agentic AI EngineerProduction discipline most candidates lack; you have shipped agentsFramework depth (LangGraph), agent evals, system design vocabulary
      GenAI / LLM EngineerAWS and data foundationsLLM fundamentals, prompt and model evaluation, fine-tuning concepts
      How to phrase it in an interview

      "I treat an agent system as a data system with a non-deterministic component in the middle. So I apply what I do for pipelines: idempotency, lineage through traces, access control in the data layer, cost per unit of work, and quality gates, which here are evals. On top of that I've learned what is specific to models: context management, tool design, and evaluating meaning."

      Interview: You're a data engineer. Why should we hire you for an agentic AI role?

      "Because the hard part of agents in production is the part I already do. Agents fail on stale or badly modelled data, missing access control, non-idempotent actions, runaway cost and no testing, and those are data-engineering problems. I've run production pipelines on Glue, Iceberg and Step Functions as the sole engineer, so I own reliability end to end. And I haven't only read about agents: I've built an assistant over Athena, Confluence and Jira that unblocked a six-month-old problem in about an hour, a migration agent with human approval between planning and code generation, and a multi-agent PR reviewer that took second place in a company-wide hackathon. What I add to a team is agents that are grounded in governed data and that I can prove work, with evals and traces."

      Interview: What's the biggest mindset change moving from pipelines to agents?

      "Accepting non-determinism and designing around it. In a pipeline, same input means same output and a test is an equality check. With a model in the loop, I measure pass rates on a dataset, I assume any single call can be wrong, and I put deterministic guards around it: schema validation, SQL parsing, permission checks, budgets, approvals. The second change is that text is the interface. A vague tool description or an unhelpful error message is a bug, because the model acts on it."

      Senior data engineer · hands-on

      LLM as a pipeline stage: batch enrichment at scale

      The most common GenAI task handed to a data engineer is not a chatbot. It is "classify, extract or summarise these ten million records every night". That is a transformation stage, and it should be built with the same guarantees as any other: idempotent, incremental, restartable, validated and costed.

      Which execution mode

      ModeUse whenTrade-off
      Bedrock batch inferenceThousands to millions of records, results can wait hoursLower price than on-demand; asynchronous; minimum record counts and per-file limits apply
      Step Functions Distributed Map calling the model per itemNeed results in minutes, want per-item retry and visibilityOn-demand price; set MaxConcurrency to stay under your tokens-per-minute quota
      Glue PySpark with mapPartitionsThe call is one step inside an existing Spark jobExecutors can hammer the quota: cap partitions, add backoff, reuse one client per partition
      Lambda per eventLow volume, event-driven (a file or ticket arrives)Simple; watch timeout and concurrency

      The stage, end to end

      llm_stage.py: incremental, idempotent classification with Bedrock batch inferencePython
      import hashlib, json, time, boto3

s3 = boto3.client("s3"); bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock", region_name="us-east-1")
BUCKET, MODEL_ID = "my-llm-stage", "<batch-capable model id>"
ROLE = "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/bedrock-batch-role"
PROMPT_VERSION = "ticket-triage-v3"          # change this and every row becomes "not yet done" again

PROMPT = """Classify this support ticket. Reply with JSON only:
{{"category": "billing|shipping|product|other", "urgent": true|false}}

<ticket>{text}</ticket>"""

def record_id(row_id: str, text: str) -> str:
    """Stable key: same input + same prompt version + same model => same id => safe to skip or MERGE."""
    return hashlib.sha256(f"{row_id}|{text}|{PROMPT_VERSION}|{MODEL_ID}".encode()).hexdigest()[:32]

def build_jsonl(rows: list[dict]) -> str:
    lines = []
    for r in rows:
        body = {"anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31", "max_tokens": 100, "temperature": 0,
                "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT.format(text=r["text"][:4000])}]}
        # modelInput is the model's own request body; check the docs for the format your model expects
        lines.append(json.dumps({"recordId": record_id(r["id"], r["text"]), "modelInput": body}))
    return "\n".join(lines)

def submit(rows: list[dict], run: str) -> str:
    key = f"in/{run}/batch.jsonl"
    s3.put_object(Bucket=BUCKET, Key=key, Body=build_jsonl(rows).encode())
    job = bedrock.create_model_invocation_job(
        jobName=f"triage-{run}", roleArn=ROLE, modelId=MODEL_ID,
        clientRequestToken=run,                                   # makes the submit itself idempotent
        inputDataConfig={"s3InputDataConfig": {"s3Uri": f"s3://{BUCKET}/{key}"}},
        outputDataConfig={"s3OutputDataConfig": {"s3Uri": f"s3://{BUCKET}/out/{run}/"}})
    return job["jobArn"]

def wait(job_arn: str, poll_s: int = 60) -> str:                 # in Step Functions use a Wait + Choice loop instead
    while True:
        status = bedrock.get_model_invocation_job(jobIdentifier=job_arn)["status"]
        if status in ("Completed", "PartiallyCompleted", "Failed", "Stopped", "Expired"):
            return status
        time.sleep(poll_s)

ALLOWED = {"billing", "shipping", "product", "other"}

def parse_line(line: str) -> dict:
    """One output line -> a validated row or a failure row. Never raise: bad rows go to the retry table."""
    rec = json.loads(line)
    rid = rec.get("recordId")
    try:
        text = rec["modelOutput"]["content"][0]["text"]
        data = json.loads(text[text.index("{"): text.rindex("}") + 1])
        if data["category"] not in ALLOWED or not isinstance(data["urgent"], bool):
            raise ValueError("schema")
        usage = rec["modelOutput"].get("usage", {})
        return {"record_id": rid, "ok": True, "category": data["category"], "urgent": data["urgent"],
                "in_tokens": usage.get("input_tokens", 0), "out_tokens": usage.get("output_tokens", 0),
                "prompt_version": PROMPT_VERSION, "model_id": MODEL_ID}
    except Exception as e:
        return {"record_id": rid, "ok": False, "error": str(e)[:200], "raw": json.dumps(rec)[:1000]}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    good = json.dumps({"recordId": "a1", "modelOutput": {"content": [{"text": '{"category": "billing", "urgent": true}'}],
                                                         "usage": {"input_tokens": 88, "output_tokens": 14}}})
    bad = json.dumps({"recordId": "b2", "modelOutput": {"content": [{"text": "I think it is about refunds."}]}})
    for line in (good, bad):
        print(parse_line(line))
      Output of the parser self-testOutput
      {'record_id': 'a1', 'ok': True, 'category': 'billing', 'urgent': True, 'in_tokens': 88, 'out_tokens': 14, 'prompt_version': 'ticket-triage-v3', 'model_id': '<batch-capable model id>'}
{'record_id': 'b2', 'ok': False, 'error': 'substring not found', 'raw': '{"recordId": "b2", "modelOutput": {"content": [{"text": "I think it is about refunds."}]}}'}
      Select only work not yet done, then MERGE results (Spark SQL on Iceberg)SQL
      -- 1. incremental selection: rows with no result for the current prompt + model version
SELECT t.id, t.text
FROM   glue_catalog.trusted.tickets t
LEFT ANTI JOIN glue_catalog.enriched.ticket_triage r
       ON  r.ticket_id = t.id
       AND r.prompt_version = 'ticket-triage-v3'
       AND r.model_id = '<batch-capable model id>'
WHERE  t.ingest_date >= date_sub(current_date(), 3);     -- small lookback catches late and retried rows

-- 2. idempotent write: re-running the same batch changes nothing
MERGE INTO glue_catalog.enriched.ticket_triage tgt
USING staged_results src
ON tgt.record_id = src.record_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

      Design rules

      Key by input + prompt version + model version
      That single decision gives you idempotent re-runs, selective backfills when the prompt changes, and an audit answer to "which prompt produced this value?".
      Validate every row; never fail the job on one bad row
      Bad rows go to a retry table with the raw output. Retry once on-demand with the validation error in the prompt; what still fails goes to a human queue. Track the failure rate as a data-quality metric.
      Store usage with the result
      Tokens per row lets you report cost per run and per source, and spot a prompt change that doubled cost.
      Sample for quality
      Each run, send a small random sample to a judge or a human and trend the agreement. Schema-valid is not the same as correct.
      Pre-filter with cheap logic
      Don't send rows a regex or a lookup can decide. Deduplicate identical inputs first; repeated tickets or log lines are common.
      Mask before sending
      Apply the same PHI/PII masking you use in the trusted layer before text leaves for the model, and keep the batch bucket as locked down as the source.
      Throttle on-demand fan-out
      With Distributed Map or Spark, cap concurrency from your tokens-per-minute quota: concurrency ≈ quota ÷ (tokens per call × calls per minute per worker).
      Check before you promise numbers

      Batch inference availability, discount, minimum and maximum records per job, and turnaround time differ by model and Region and change over time. Look at the current Bedrock batch inference documentation and quotas for the model you plan to use before you commit to a schedule.

      Interview: Design a nightly job that classifies 5 million support tickets with an LLM.

      "I'd build it as an incremental, idempotent stage. Select tickets that don't yet have a result for the current prompt and model version, deduplicate identical texts, and mask PII. Write requests as JSONL to S3, keyed by a hash of ticket, prompt version and model, and run Bedrock batch inference since results can wait and it's cheaper than on-demand. Step Functions submits the job, polls, then a Glue job parses the output, validates each row against the schema, and MERGEs valid rows into an Iceberg table with token usage. Invalid rows go to a retry table and get one on-demand retry. I'd sample a few hundred rows per run for a judge or human check, and alarm on failure rate, cost per run and label distribution drift. Changing the prompt version automatically triggers a backfill, which I'd run on a sample first and compare with the eval set."

      Interview: You call a model from inside a PySpark job and get throttled constantly. Why, and what do you do?

      "Spark parallelism multiplies requests: every executor and partition calls the model at once, so I exceed the tokens-per-minute quota immediately, and retries make it worse. Fixes: use mapPartitions with one client per partition and backoff with jitter, coalesce to a partition count sized from the quota, and deduplicate inputs first. Better, move the calls out of Spark: write the inputs to S3 and use batch inference, or a Step Functions Distributed Map with a concurrency limit, and keep Spark for preparing and merging data. I'd also check whether a smaller model or a cross-Region inference profile gives more headroom."

      Senior data engineer · architecture

      Building an AI-ready lakehouse

      Agents are only as good as the data and metadata they can reach. "AI-ready" means four concrete things on a lakehouse: metadata an agent can read, an embedding pipeline that stays fresh, governance the agent inherits, and a tool layer over the platform. This is the work an Agentic AI Data Engineer is hired to do.

      1. Metadata is now context

      A text-to-SQL agent reads your Glue Data Catalog the way a new analyst would. If a column is called stts_cd with no comment, the agent guesses. The cheapest quality improvement on any data assistant is writing descriptions.

      MetadataWhere it livesWhat the agent does with it
      Table and column descriptionsGlue Data Catalog commentsFinds the right table, picks the right column
      Allowed values and unitsColumn comment or a reference tableWrites correct filters (status = 'FAILED', not 'failed')
      Join keys and grainTable description, or a relationships tableAvoids fan-out joins and double counting
      Business definitions (metrics)Semantic layer, curated views, glossaryUses the certified definition of "active customer"
      Freshness and ownerTable properties, audit tableTells the user how current the answer is and who to ask
      Sensitivity tagsLake Formation LF-TagsNever selects or shows restricted columns
      Example queriesA table of question → SQL pairsFew-shot examples retrieved by similarity
      Export the catalog as documents for a metadata index (one document per table)Python
      import boto3
glue = boto3.client("glue")

def table_documents(database: str) -> list[dict]:
    docs = []
    for page in glue.get_paginator("get_tables").paginate(DatabaseName=database):
        for t in page["TableList"]:
            cols = t["StorageDescriptor"]["Columns"] + t.get("PartitionKeys", [])
            part = {c["Name"] for c in t.get("PartitionKeys", [])}
            undocumented = [c["Name"] for c in cols if not c.get("Comment")]
            lines = [f'- {c["Name"]} ({c["Type"]}){" [partition]" if c["Name"] in part else ""}: {c.get("Comment", "NO DESCRIPTION")}'
                     for c in cols]
            docs.append({
                "id": f'{database}.{t["Name"]}',
                "text": f'Table {database}.{t["Name"]}\n{t.get("Description", "NO DESCRIPTION")}\nColumns:\n' + "\n".join(lines),
                "metadata": {"database": database, "owner": t.get("Owner", ""), "format": t.get("Parameters", {}).get("table_type", ""),
                             "undocumented_columns": len(undocumented)},
            })
    return docs

if __name__ == "__main__":
    docs = table_documents("trusted")
    worst = sorted(docs, key=lambda d: -d["metadata"]["undocumented_columns"])[:10]
    for d in worst:                               # your documentation backlog, ranked
        print(d["id"], d["metadata"]["undocumented_columns"])

      Embed these documents into a small index and you have the find_tables tool from the text-to-SQL lesson. The "undocumented columns" count is a metric worth putting on a dashboard: it is a leading indicator of agent quality.

      2. The embedding pipeline is a normal incremental pipeline

      Keep embeddings in the lake too
      Store chunks and vectors in Iceberg as the system of record, and treat the vector database as a serving copy you can rebuild. That gives you time travel, cheap re-loads into a different store, and Athena queries over your own index ("how many chunks per document?", "which documents were never embedded?").
      Change detection
      Chunk key = hash of document ID and chunk text. An anti-join between today's chunks and the embeddings table gives exactly the chunks to embed; a reverse anti-join gives the chunks to delete.
      Deletes and versions
      When a document is replaced, old chunks must leave the serving index in the same run, or the agent will quote the superseded policy. Reconcile counts between the Iceberg table and the index, as you do between layers today.
      Model change = new table
      Partition or name embeddings by model. Never mix. Build the new index beside the old one, evaluate, switch.
      Access metadata travels with the chunk
      Team, tenant, sensitivity. The retrieval query filters on it.
      Freshness SLA
